c1_dawn_spin.text:
Dawn came to the lower city the way it always did, gray and reluctant, sliding under the dish-hall's warped door before it touched anything else. Rin was already there. They were always there first, in the hour when the dishes were empty and the chalk dust hung undisturbed and the hall smelled of cold iron and old rosin and the river two streets over.

They set the blade against the launcher cord and breathed.

The blade was chipped along one rim, a hairline scar that caught the light wrong. It had no maker's mark, no spirit-crest, no name etched into its crown the way the good blades had. Someone, years ago, had thrown it into a bin of spares no one wanted, and a smaller Rin had fished it out because it was the one thing in the orphan dish-hall that nobody would ever ask for back. That was the whole of its value, once. It had become something else since.

"Ready?" Rin asked it, very quietly, the way you ask a friend a question you already know the answer to.

The morning held its breath.

Three. Two. One.

"Spirits, fly."

The cord ripped free and the blade dropped onto the dish and bit, and the small sick wobble that lived under Rin's ribs all day — the one that came from too many doors closing — went still. It always went still here. For as long as the blade spun, there was a steady silver hum at the center of the world, and Rin stood inside it, and for once nothing was leaving.
c1_dawn_spin.title: The Chipped Blade

c1_the_answer.text:
The blade carved its slow circles and Rin watched it the way other children watched the harbor, looking for something coming home.

Low in the spin, where the metal blurred into a smear of motion, there was a shape. Not a trick of the eye — Rin had learned the difference years ago. A long, lean curve of something that wasn't the blade, that turned when the blade turned and listened when Rin spoke. Faint. Always faint. But there.

"Stay with it," Rin murmured, and the hum deepened, just slightly, the way a sleeper shifts toward a familiar voice. That was the thing no one believed when Rin tried to explain it, back when Rin still tried. The blade answered. It had answered since the first dawn they'd brought it down here, alone, and talked to it because there was no one else to talk to and the silence had teeth.

It answered. It had never once given its name.

Every bonded blade in the world carried a beast that, when it truly trusted its spinner, spoke the name only that spinner could hear. Rin had read it in the Warden-tracts, heard it in the dish-hall lessons. A name was the proof. A name was the beast saying: I have chosen you, and I am staying.

The chipped blade had spun under Rin's hands for six years and given them everything but that.

Rin had stopped reading it as a mystery a long time ago. They read it the only way that made sense. The bond was broken somewhere, cracked like the rim, and a cracked thing didn't hold. Nothing held, not all the way. You learned that or you learned nothing.

c1_pae_arrives.text:
The door banged. Rin did not flinch — they had heard the footsteps coming up the lane, had already counted them, already known there was only one set and that they were small and quick and uneven on the left foot.

"You started without me," said Pae, breathless, clutching a launcher to their chest like something that might bolt. "You always start without me."

"You're always late."

"I'm not late, the sun's barely up." Pae dropped onto the bench beside the dish and watched Rin's blade with naked hunger, chin on fists. Pae was younger by three winters and shorter by a head and had followed Rin out of the orphan hall the way a smaller blade gets pulled into the wake of a bigger one. "How do you make it do that. The hum. Mine just rattles and dies."

"You're gripping the cord too tight. You're telling it what to do instead of asking."

"That's the same thing."

"It really isn't." Rin caught the blade as its spin slowed, palmed it warm out of the air, and for a moment Pae's whole face was turned up at them, lit with that look — the one that said Rin had hung the morning sky. Rin felt the old reflexive step backward in their chest, the half-inch of distance they put between themself and anyone who looked at them like that. Not because Pae was unwelcome. Because the people who looked at you like that were the ones it cost the most to lose, and Rin had been very thoroughly taught how that ended. "Here," they said instead, and set the chipped blade in Pae's hands. "Feel how it's still turning a little, even stopped? That's it deciding whether to trust you. Don't grab. Just hold."

Pae held it like it was made of glass and light. "It's warm."

"Yeah," Rin said. "It is."

c1_stranger_watches.text:
Rin noticed the man before Pae did, because Rin noticed everyone.

It was a habit older than memory: read the room, read the faces, find the exits, find the moment a kind expression starts to curdle into the one that means you've stayed too long. Rin had three exits mapped in this hall before they could spell. So the stranger by the far pillar registered the instant he went still — an older man, broad-shouldered and gone a little soft with years, in a traveler's coat too plain to be anyone's and too clean to be no one's. He had been passing. He had stopped.

He was watching Rin talk to the blade.

Not the way the dish-hall master watched, measuring whether you'd be worth the bread you ate. Not the way the Concord scouts watched on their rare slumming visits, pricing you. He watched the way a person watches a thing they had given up on ever seeing again — carefully, as if it might startle and bolt if he moved.

Rin met his eyes. Most adults looked away when an orphan caught them staring; there was always that little flinch of being caught pitying. This man didn't look away. He inclined his head, very slightly, as if Rin had done something worth acknowledging, and Rin had no idea what.

"Who's that?" Pae whispered, finally following Rin's gaze.

"No one," Rin said, which was what they said about everyone, because no one was the safest thing a person could be. They took the blade gently back from Pae's hands. The hum had gone out of it. Just metal now, dull and quiet, the way it always went when it wasn't turning — the way Rin privately believed everything went, in the end, when you stopped holding it up.

c1_the_offer.text:
The man crossed the hall slowly, the way you approach a stray, and stopped a careful distance off — far enough that Rin's shoulders didn't climb.

"That blade has no name on it," he said. His voice was low and worn smooth, like river-stone. "And it answers you anyway."

Rin said nothing. Pae looked between them, delighted and confused.

"Most people can't hear a beast that hasn't given its name," the man went on. "They decide there's nothing there to hear. You talk to it like it's listening." He paused. "It's listening."

Something turned over in Rin's chest, hard, and they crushed it flat out of pure reflex. "It's a hand-me-down," Rin said. "It's chipped. It doesn't even spin true past a minute."

"No," the man agreed. "It doesn't." He looked at the blade, and then at Rin, and there was something in his face that Rin couldn't file under any of the usual headings — not pity, not appraisal. Recognition, maybe, though Rin couldn't have said of what. "The Bond Tournament opens in Coilspire in six weeks. Single elimination. The Spiral Crown to whoever wins it." A beat. "And money. Enough to leave the lower city for good. Enough that no one ever decides your bed is needed for someone else."

Rin went very still. He had said it too precisely. He knew exactly which wound he was pressing, and he'd pressed it like a man who'd carried the same one a long time.

"I could train you for it," the man said. "You and that nameless blade. I think you'd surprise the whole city."

c1_reaction_choice.text: It was a beautiful door, swinging open. Rin had learned, before they'd learned much else, exactly how to walk away from beautiful doors. The word no was already shaped in their mouth — easy, automatic, the cleanest exit in the room.

choices.label: Guarded — ask what he gets out of it
Honest — admit the blade is all they have

c1_react_guard.text:
"What do you get out of it?"

The question came out flat and hard, the voice Rin used to make grown-ups remember they were talking to someone who couldn't be easily moved. Pae winced at the rudeness of it. The man didn't.

"That's the right question," he said, and to Rin's surprise he looked almost pleased, as though they'd passed something. "Smart, to ask it. Most kids your age hear 'crown' and 'money' and stop listening." He turned the traveler's coat tighter against the morning chill, buying a moment. "What I get is — " He stopped. Started again, plainer. "I trained someone, a long time ago. It went wrong, in a way I've never been able to set right. I'd like to do it once more before I'm done, and do it better. That's the whole of it. You can believe me or not."

It was not the answer of a man trying to sell something. There was no shine on it. Rin had heard a thousand pitches in this hall — recruiters, fosters, do-gooders — and every one of them had glowed with how good it would be. This one didn't glow. It ached.

That, more than any promise, was what made Rin keep listening. A person who wanted something from you smiled. A person who had lost something looked exactly like this.

"I'm not easy to teach," Rin warned, which was the closest they could come, just then, to not saying no.

c1_react_honest.text:
The no didn't come. What came instead surprised Rin so much they nearly stepped back from their own mouth.

"It's the only thing I've got," they said. Quietly. Looking at the blade and not the man, because it was easier to be honest with the blade in the room. "People got returned to the hall, growing up. Things got taken back. This didn't. It's the one thing that never — " The sentence ran out of floor and Rin let it drop. "If I take it to a tournament and it cracks the rest of the way, I don't get it back. So you'll understand if I don't hand it to a stranger because he says the word crown."

For a long moment the man said nothing at all. Pae had gone very quiet, the way kids go quiet when grown-up things move through a room over their heads.

"No," the man said at last, and his voice had gone rough. "I do understand that. Better than you'd think." He looked at the chipped blade in Rin's hands as though it were something he half-recognized. "I'm not asking you to risk it on my word. I'm telling you it's stronger than you believe, and so are you, and that a thing which has stayed with you this long has already proven the only thing that matters about it."

Rin's throat did something complicated. They mastered it. "That's a lot of faith," they managed, "in a blade you watched die after one minute."

"I've seen blades worth less win everything," the man said. "And blades worth everything lose. The difference was never the blade."

c1_the_world.text:
Pae had drifted to the hall's far wall, where the past hung peeling. Rin followed, half to think, half to put a little distance between themself and the size of what was being offered.

The wall was a graveyard of the sport. A Concord poster, new enough that its corners still held — MODERN WEAVING, it read over a spinner in a sleek grey coat, NO BOND REQUIRED. EFFICIENT. PROVEN. The figure's blade threw off clean geometric light, and there was something in the image Rin had never been able to name and didn't like, a coldness, a blade that obeyed instead of answered.

Beside it, far older, curling off the brick: a Bond Tournament banner from some long-gone year, its spiral crest faded to a ghost. ONLY THE TRUE MAY ENTER. The cloth had gone the color of dust.

"The masters at the hall say the old way's finished," Pae said, tracing the spiral with one finger. "They say the ones who win now don't even bond. They use — " Pae lowered their voice, the way you do for a word that scares you. " — cold signs. Andro from the next street said his cousin spun against one and his cousin's blade just... went wrong. Like the spirit in it got scared."

Behind them, the man had gone still again. Rin felt it more than saw it — the particular stillness of someone who knows exactly what a word means and wishes a child didn't have to.

"That's enough about that," the man said, gently, and Pae went quiet. But the word had landed in the room and stayed there, cold under everything, the way the river-damp stayed in the walls.

c1_decision.text:
The man left them to think — stepped out into the lane, where Rin could see him through the warped window standing with his hands in his coat, looking at nothing, waiting without pretending he wasn't.

Rin sat back down at the dish and held the chipped blade in both hands. It was cold and dull and silent, just metal, the way it always was when it wasn't turning. The hairline scar ran along the rim under their thumb, familiar as a scar on their own skin.

"He thinks you've got a name in there," Rin told it, under their breath, so Pae wouldn't hear. "After six years. He thinks you've just been waiting."

The blade said nothing, because of course it did. It never said anything when it was still. That was the whole problem, wasn't it. That was the thing Rin had decided about it years ago, and about everything: that what doesn't speak its name isn't yours to keep, and you'd better not let yourself believe otherwise, because believing was where it always started to hurt.

And yet.

It had stayed. Whatever else was true, whatever the lessons said about names and proof and broken bonds — the dull cold thing in their hands had been there every single dawn, when nothing and no one else had. Rin thought about the man's face. I'd like to do it once more before I'm done. Rin thought about a poster that promised a blade you'd never have to need.

Pae was watching them, holding their breath, not even pretending not to hope.

Rin stood up. The wobble in their chest was loud now, fear and something dangerously close to wanting. They walked to the door anyway. "Alright," they said to the waiting man, before they could talk themself out of it. "Teach me."

c2_arrival.text:
The hill-town smelled nothing like home. Where the lower-city dish-halls had reeked of hot metal and chalk and the sour breath of too many bodies pressed into too little room, the air here was thin and clean and tasted faintly of pine, and Rin distrusted it the way they distrusted anything that asked for nothing in return. The Coach's training hall was a barn that had given up being a barn — swept clean, the old stalls knocked out, a single battered practice dish set into the floor like a healed-over wound. Light came in slantwise through gaps in the planking and laid bright bars across the dust.

Rin set their bag down by the door, then moved it a hand's width closer to the threshold without thinking. Old habit. A bag near the door was a bag you could grab on the way out, and Rin had learned a long time ago to know where the out was before they learned anything else about a room.

The Coach noticed. Rin could tell by the way his eyes went to the bag and then, deliberately, away — not commenting, just filing it somewhere. He was a broad, weathered man who moved like he was carrying something heavy that no one else could see, and he had a way of looking at Rin that made the wobble start up in their chest, the small private flutter of being seen too clearly.

"You came," he said, as if it were a thing worth remarking on. As if Rin's coming had cost something he understood.

"You offered," Rin said.

"People offer a lot of things." He turned toward the dish. "Come. Show me how you launch."
c2_arrival.title: The Six Signs

c2_launch_test.text:
Rin drew the chipped blade from its wrap and felt, as always, the small click of rightness when it sat in their palm — the one weight in the world that had never been taken back. Up close it was an ugly thing. A no-name hand-me-down, the rim notched where some forgotten owner had let it strike stone, the spirit-motif worn to a ghost of itself. Nobody had wanted it. That was precisely why Rin trusted it.

They fitted it to the launcher, threaded the cord, and set their feet at the dish's edge the way they had ten thousand mornings. The old count rose in them without being asked.

"Three," Rin breathed. "Two. One." Then, quieter than the words deserved, the cry that every spinner in the world was taught before they were taught anything else: "Spirits, fly."

The cord ripped free. The blade dropped, bit, and spun — and the hall filled with the low true note of a good launch, that singing hum Rin would have known in their sleep. In the blur of it, if you looked the way Rin had taught themselves to look, you could almost see the shape that lived inside: a faint beast-curl of light, there and not there, turning when the blade turned.

The Coach watched it for a long moment. Something moved across his face — not surprise. Recognition, maybe, of a kind that hurt.

"Clean," he said at last. "Cleaner than half the cold-style cadets in Coilspire." He crouched at the dish's rim, eye-level with the spinning blade. "But you launch it like a stone you're throwing. Not like a thing you're talking to."

Rin's jaw tightened. "It spins."

"Spinning isn't the lesson," he said. "Listening is."

c2_first_spin_myth.text:
He let the blade run down on its own, and when it finally wobbled and dropped and lay still, he picked it up and turned it in his thick fingers with a gentleness that surprised Rin — the way you might hold a sleeping animal.

"You know the First Spin," he said. It wasn't a question; every child knew it. But he told it anyway, the way the old people told it, slow, half-myth and half-physics. "At the heart of everything there was a single blade of light, turning. It threw off sparks as it spun, and the sparks cooled, and each cooled spark became a spirit-beast. Fox. Wolf. Eagle. Ten thousand kinds. Too vast to live in the world the way we do — so they learned to nest in things that turn with intent. A mill wheel. A spun coin. A child's top." He set the chipped blade on his palm. "A battle-blade."

Rin had heard it a hundred times. They had never heard it said like a man saying grace.

"It isn't only a sport," the Coach said. "Out there they'll tell you it's a sport. Sponsors, brackets, crowns. But underneath the noise it's the oldest faith we have — the belief that something will turn alongside you if you turn honestly enough." His mouth twisted, briefly, at some private cost. "That's the part they're forgetting now. That's the part I'm going to teach you to remember."

Rin looked at the dead blade in his hand and thought, as they always thought, of the thing they never said aloud: that the beast inside it had answered them since they were nine, faintly, in a way it answered no one — and had never once given its name. And that a beast that won't tell you its name is a beast that hasn't decided to stay.

They said none of it. They held out their hand for the blade. "Teach me, then."

c2_six_signs_intro.text:
"Spirit-weaving," the Coach said, "is six signs. Listen, Steady, Turn, Open, Hold, Release." He shaped each as he named it — his hands moving through the air in slow deliberate forms, fingers curling and spreading, and even empty-handed there was a weight to the motions, like he was kneading something invisible. "Most cadets are taught them as commands. Do this and the blade does that." He shook his head. "That's not what they are. They're not orders. They're one half of a conversation. You make the sign, and you wait, and the beast answers — or it doesn't."

"A conversation," Rin repeated, careful. "With a thing that can't talk."

"With a thing that talks in everything but words." He folded his hands. "Listen comes first, and it's the one everyone skips. Make the sign, then go quiet inside and feel what the blade is feeling. A beast has a temper — a nature, a defining feeling it carries. You can't weave with it until you've felt that feeling as your own." He nodded at the launcher. "Spin it again. This time don't tell it anything. Just listen."

Rin spun. They knelt, the way he had, and made the Listen sign — two fingers drawing inward toward the chest, the gather — and went still.

At first, nothing. Then, faint as a draft under a door, they felt it: the blade's feeling, seeping up the cord and into their hands. Not the spin. The mood of the thing inside.

It was lonely.

Rin had felt it before without ever letting themselves name it. Now, with the Coach watching, it landed full and undeniable — a hollow patient ache, the feeling of a thing that had waited a very long time and learned not to expect. Their throat went tight.

"There," the Coach said softly. "You heard it. Most people never do."

c2_steady_turn.text:
They worked through the morning and into the white afternoon, and to Rin's quiet astonishment the signs came easily — easily in a way almost nothing in their life had ever come.

Steady was second: a flat open palm pressed down, level, slow. It told the beast you were not going to bolt, that the ground under this turning was solid. Rin made it and felt the blade's wobble smooth, the loneliness inside it settling a half-degree, as if something had stopped bracing for a blow. They were good at this, Rin realized with a strange ache. Of course they were. They had spent their whole life being the steady one — useful, small, undemanding, the kid who never made a fuss so no one would have a reason to send them back. Their hands knew how to say I won't be a problem before they knew anything else.

Turn came third, and it was almost joyful — a rolling spiral of the wrist that asked the beast to move with you, to take the spin somewhere together. The blade chased it across the dish, light leaping in the blur, and for a few breaths Rin forgot to count the exits at all.

Hold was fifth, and it was a closed fist drawn slowly to the heart: keep what we have, don't let it scatter. Rin made it and the spin gathered, dense and bright, refusing to die.

"Good," the Coach kept saying, and each time the word landed somewhere Rin didn't have armor for. "Good. Good."

Four signs. Four of the six, and Rin had them in an afternoon — Listen, Steady, Turn, Hold. Release, the last, the Coach said they'd save. He stood back, arms crossed, and there was a brightness in his eyes that Rin didn't trust because they wanted it too much.

"You've got a gift," he said.

"There's still one left," Rin said.

His face changed. "Yes," he said. "There is."

c2_open_intro.text:
"Open," the Coach said, and made the sign — but slowly, like a man approaching something that had hurt him before. The hand came up flat against the chest, fingers together; then, all at once, it spread and turned outward, palm bared to the dish. An offering. A door with nothing behind it but you.

"The others ask the beast to do something," he said. "Move with me. Steady. Hold. Open asks nothing." He let the bared hand hang in the air. "Open lets the beast in. It's not a command and it can't be faked, because there's nothing to fake — you're not doing anything to the blade. You're letting it see you. All of you. The parts you'd rather it didn't." He lowered his hand. "It's the hardest of the six. Some spinners never get it at all. The deep form of it — the old masters called it the open-hand weave — is nearly lost now, because nobody wants to be seen that badly anymore."

Rin looked at the bared palm and felt their stomach drop in a way no physical fall had ever managed.

"Try it," he said.

They spun the blade. They knelt. They made the first four signs and felt the beast answer each one, the lonely patient thing inside leaning toward them through the cord. And then Rin lifted their hand to make Open — flat to the chest, ready to spread it outward, ready to bare the door —

and stopped.

It was only a hand. It was only air. There was no one in the barn but the Coach and a blade nobody else had wanted. And still Rin's whole body locked against it, every old instinct slamming the door before it could open, the wobble in their chest roaring up into something that was almost panic. Let it see all of you. The parts you'd rather it didn't.

Rin's hand stayed closed.

c2_open_fails.text:
"It's all right," the Coach said. "Again."

Rin tried again. And again. Each time, the first four signs flowed clean as water — and each time, when their hand rose to make Open, something in them clenched and the gesture came out wrong: too fast, too shallow, a hand thrown open like a card slapped down rather than a door eased back. And each time they faked it, the blade answered the lie.

It went flat.

That was the only word for it. The singing hum dropped to a dead grey drone, the light in the blur guttered, the beast's lonely warmth drew back and away from them the way a tide pulls off a beach — not angry, just absent, just gone, leaving Rin kneeling over a blade that spun like any other lump of metal in the world. Every time they reached for Open and didn't mean it, the one thing that had never left them turned its back.

Rin caught the blade, and their hands weren't quite steady. "It doesn't work," they said, and hated how thin it came out.

"It works," the Coach said. "You're just not letting it." He crouched beside them, slow, and didn't touch them, which somehow made it worse. "That blade's been answering you for years. Faintly. You told me that yourself."

"Faintly," Rin said. "It's never — " They stopped. Said it. "It's never told me its name."

The Coach was quiet for a moment. "A beast gives its name when it's decided to be known," he said. "And to be known, it has to know you back. All the way. You've been letting it see four-sixths of you, Rin. You've been spinning with the door held shut." He looked at the flat, sulking blade. "It's not broken. Neither are you. You just never learned to open the last sign — because the last sign is the one nobody ever let you practice."

c2_cold_sign.text:
Rin's frustration cracked into something sharper. "Then show me a way to make it answer. There has to be a faster way. Something that just — works."

The Coach went very still.

For a long moment he didn't speak. When he did, his voice had changed — gone flat and careful, the voice of a man stepping somewhere he'd sworn off. "There is," he said. "I'll show it to you once. And then you'll understand why you must never use it."

He took the launcher himself. His big hands set the chipped blade, drew the cord, and launched — "Spirits, fly" — and Rin's blade dropped into the dish spinning under someone else's will for the first time in years. The Coach knelt. And he made a sign Rin had never seen.

It looked almost like Open. That was the horror of it — it began the same, the hand rising to the chest. But where Open spread and bared, this sign clenched. The fingers hooked. The wrist gave a small cruel twist, like wringing a cloth, and the gesture turned inward and down, taking instead of offering. Rin felt the temperature of the room drop. Not really — but the air over the dish went thin and wrong, a cold under-feeling that crawled up the back of their neck.

The blade screamed.

Not a sound a person could hear. A sound Rin felt, in the place where they'd felt the loneliness — a high thin note of pure recoil. The light in the blur flinched, hard, snapping as far from the Coach's hand as the small dish would allow, cowering at the rim. The spin, though — the spin doubled. The blade tore around the dish faster and harder than Rin had ever driven it, savage and brilliant and obedient.

And utterly, sickeningly wrong.

c2_cold_sign_forbid.text:
The Coach broke the sign at once. He sat back on his heels and let the blade run wild until its forced spin spent itself and it clattered to a stop, and when he picked it up his hand was not quite steady either. The lonely warmth crept back into the blur slowly, warily, the way a beaten dog comes back to a doorway.

"That," he said, "is a cold sign."

Rin's mouth was dry. "It flinched away from you. It was afraid of you."

"Yes." He set the blade down between them. "A cold sign doesn't ask. It compels. It takes the beast's power without its consent, and it works — Spirits, it works, you saw it, twice the spin and none of the trust. A cold-style master can beat almost anyone in this world." His jaw worked. "And every time they use it, the beast goes a little deaf to them. Stops answering. Draws back, and back, and back, until one day the spinner makes a sign and nothing comes — and they're standing in the middle of a packed arena, winning, perfectly alone, holding a blade that will never speak to them again."

"Has that — " Rin started.

"It's happening right now," the Coach said, "to half the children Concord trains, and they're calling it progress." He met Rin's eyes. "Promise me you will never weave a cold sign. Not to win. Not to wake a stubborn blade. Not when you're losing and there's a way out and the whole crowd is screaming. Never."

"How do you know it so well?" Rin asked. "You wove it like — "

"Promise me," the Coach said, and there was something underneath the words, something old and raw, a door of his own held very firmly shut. He would not say how he knew. He would not say anything at all.

"I promise," Rin said.

He nodded once, and looked away, and the subject closed like a wound.

c2_train_choice.text:
They went back to Open. Of course they went back to Open — there was no path around it, only through. Afternoon bled toward evening, the slanting light reddening on the floorboards, and the blade went flat under Rin's closed hand again and again and again. The Coach said little now. He had said the things that could be said. The rest, Rin understood, was theirs alone to do.

Standing over the sulking blade, Rin felt the old fork in the road that every hard thing in their life had come down to — and felt, this time, that it was theirs to choose.

choices.label: Slow down. Make it a thousand times, patiently, until your hands stop lying.
Stop holding back. Throw yourself straight at the hardest sign, all at once.

c2_train_patient.text:
Rin let their shoulders drop. Slowly, then. The way they did everything — small, careful, one quiet repetition at a time, the way you wear a path into stone by walking it ten thousand mornings.

They stopped trying to fling the door open. Instead they made the Open sign as slowly as a person can make a gesture — the hand rising to the chest, holding there, the fingers easing apart by degrees, the palm turning outward a breath at a time. They didn't ask the blade for anything. They just let one true thing leak through the gap before they closed it again: the loneliness. Their own, this time — not the beast's. The kid by the door with the bag set for a quick exit. The thing they had never let anyone see.

The blade didn't blaze. It didn't speak. But for one heartbeat, before Rin's instincts shut the door, the dead grey drone lifted — just barely, just a half-tone — and the lonely warmth in the blur leaned toward them instead of away.

Then it was gone, and the blade was only a blade again.

But Rin had felt it. The smallest possible answer. A foot in the door before the door swung shut.

The Coach, watching from the shadows, let out a slow breath. "There," he said, very quietly, almost to himself. "There it is."

Rin didn't trust their voice. They reset the blade, and set their feet, and made the sign again — slower still. Patience was the one tool they'd always had. They had outlasted every home that sent them back. They could outlast a closed door, even their own.

c2_train_reckless.text:
No. Rin was done easing toward it. They had eased toward everything their whole life — kept small, kept careful, kept the door cracked an inch and never more — and it had won them exactly nothing but a blade that wouldn't say its name.

They set the blade spinning hard and dropped to the dish and tore through the first four signs fast, faster than the Coach had taught, and when their hand reached Open they did not hold back the way they always held back. They flung the door wide. All of it. The orphanage that sent them away twice. The bag by the door. The terror, bared raw to a chipped blade in a stranger's barn — here, this is me, this is the whole ugly shape of it, look —

The blade reared.

It was too much, too fast — the spin lurched, the light in the blur flared and bucked, and for a sickening instant Rin felt the beast recoil from the sheer flood of it, the way you flinch from a door thrown open in your face. The hum cracked. The blade skidded wild and leapt the rim and clattered across the floorboards into the shadows.

Silence.

Rin knelt there, chest heaving, hands shaking, more open and more exposed than they had been in years — and the blade lay dark in the corner, spun out.

But it had not gone flat. That was the thing. It hadn't turned its back the way it did when Rin faked the sign. It had been overwhelmed — overwhelmed, which meant it had felt the truth of what Rin flung at it, all of it, no lie in the gesture at all.

The Coach crossed to the blade and picked it up and turned it over, and there was wonder in his weathered face, and something close to fear. "Too much," he said. "But real. The whole door at once." He looked at Rin a long moment. "You're going to be a problem for everyone who ever taught a cadet to keep their hand half-closed."

c2_refrain.text:
It was full dark by the time they stopped. The slanting bars of light were gone; the barn held only the small gold of a hanging lantern, and the dish lay quiet, and Rin's hands ached in a clean, used-up way they hadn't felt in a long time. They had not mastered Open. They both knew it. The last sign was still a door Rin could only crack, not swing — but they had cracked it, and a crack was more than the blade had ever been given before.

The Coach wrapped the chipped blade in its cloth with that surprising gentleness and held it out. Rin took it, and the small click of rightness came as it always did — but tonight there was something else under it, the faintest hum, as if the thing inside had not entirely gone back to sleep.

"You'll never win the Tournament on the first five signs," the Coach said. "Every cold-style cadet in Coilspire has the first five. They'll be faster than you, most of them. Harder. They'll have blades that didn't come out of a scrap bin." He picked up his own bag, slung it over one heavy shoulder, and paused at the door — and Rin noticed, with a small lurch, that their own bag still sat exactly where they'd nudged it, half a hand from the threshold, ready to grab and run.

"The sixth sign is the only thing they can't take from you," he said. "And it's the one that scares you most. I know." His eyes went to the bag by the door, and back. He didn't mention it. He only said the thing he would say to Rin a hundred more times before the end, the thing Rin could not yet believe, the thing the whole rest of the story would spend itself proving true:

"A blade wobbles when it spins alone."

He stepped out into the dark. After a moment, Rin picked up the bag — and carried it deeper into the room, away from the door, before they followed.

c3_arrival.text:
The train shed had emptied them out into a tunnel that smelled of coal and wet stone, and then the tunnel had ended, and Coilspire happened all at once.

Rin stopped walking. They had to. The Coliseum filled the whole top of the world ahead of them, a ring of pale tiered stone so vast it seemed less built than grown, banner-cloth snapping along its rim in colors Rin had no names for. The roar came down off it in a single unbroken wave — thousands of voices folded into one sound, the sound a crowd makes when it has forgotten it is made of people. Rin felt it in the soles of their feet through the chipped blade in their coat pocket, a low pressure against the breastbone where the wobble lived.

They had spun alone in a dish-hall the size of this gate's shadow. The thought arrived without permission, the way the bad thoughts always did, and Rin let it pass through and counted, instead, the exits: the tunnel behind, the stairs left, the wide processional ahead choked with people who all seemed to know exactly where they were going. Three. Three ways out. The counting steadied them. It always had.

A tailings kid in a coat two seasons too short, standing at the foot of a thing built for champions. Rin tightened their grip on the blade, the chip in its rim catching their thumb the way it had every day for six years, a small familiar hurt, the one thing that had never once been taken back. The crowd-roar swelled and broke. Somewhere up inside that pale ring, the Bond Tournament was already deciding who belonged. Rin made themself breathe and started up the steps.
c3_arrival.title: The Coliseum Gate

c3_pae_tagalong.text:
"It's bigger than the whole borough," Pae said, somewhere around Rin's elbow. "It's bigger than the SKY."

Pae had not, technically, been invited. Pae had simply appeared on the platform that morning with a satchel and a wobbling beginner blade and an expression that dared anyone to send them back, which was an expression Rin recognized, because it was the one they had worn at nine and never since admitted to. They hadn't had the heart to argue. That was the trouble with Pae. They walked straight through the half-step of distance Rin kept around everyone like it wasn't even there.

"Stay close," Rin said. "Crowds like this, people get separated." It came out flatter than they meant. What they meant was something they didn't have the words for and wouldn't have said if they did — something about how easy it was to lose a person in a place this size, how you could turn around and they'd be gone, and the world would simply close over the space where they'd been.

Pae beamed as though Rin had promised them something. "You're going to win the whole thing," they said. "And then we'll have the money and nobody can send anybody anywhere ever again."

Rin almost corrected the we. The prize was a way out of the lower city — one way out, sized for one person. But Pae was looking up at the banners with their whole hungry face open to the sun, and Rin found they couldn't do it. "Stay close," they said again, gentler this time, and let the rest go unspoken, and pretended the small warm ache under their ribs was just the long climb.

c3_registration.text:
The registration hall was a cavern of echoing marble where clerks sat behind a long counter like judges who had grown bored of judging. Rin found the line for open challengers — shorter than the others, and worse dressed — and waited, and rehearsed, and when their turn came they set their papers on the counter and their chipped blade beside them with the careful flourish of someone presenting a credential.

The marshal of the gate looked at the blade for a long moment. He was old in the way the building was old, polished and unimpressed, with a Concord pin glinting at his collar. He did not pick up Rin's papers. He picked up the blade, turned it once in the cold light, and set it down a half-inch from where it had been, as if even that contact required washing off.

"This is a hand-me-down," he said. "No house mark. No registry. The rolls require a blade of provenance." He smiled without using his eyes. "Where did a tailings child come by a battle-blade at all?"

The hall seemed to lean in. Behind Rin the line shuffled; somewhere a clerk stamped something with a sound like a small door closing. Rin had been made small before, in registries and intake offices and the doorways of houses that had decided, after all, not to keep them — and the old reflex rose, the one that said make yourself smaller still, agree, apologize, take up no room. Their thumb found the chip in the rim. Six years that blade had answered them when nothing else would. Provenance. As if a thing had to come from somewhere to be worth keeping. As if Rin did.

c3_oru.text:
"The rolls require a true bond," said a voice, dry as turning pages. "Provenance is a Concord word. It is not in the law."

She came out from a side door without hurry — a small robed woman, ancient, an old Tournament emblem worked into her collar in thread gone silver with age. Her eyes were clouded, the whites gone soft and milky, and yet when they settled on Rin they seemed to see more than the marshal's had, not less. The marshal straightened the way men straighten for someone they have been outranked by for years and resent it freshly each time.

"Warden Oru," he said. "This is registry business."

"It is law business, and the law is mine." She did not raise her voice. She set two fingers on Rin's blade — light, almost tender — and went still, the way the Coach went still when he listened to a beast. The cavern's noise thinned to nothing in Rin's ears. For one suspended breath Oru's clouded eyes half-closed, and Rin felt absurdly that the blade was being read like a page, and that whatever was written there was being weighed by someone who could actually read it.

"There is a bond here," Oru said at last, quietly, and something moved across her old face that might, in a younger woman, have been hope. "Faint. Unnamed. But real — and answering only to this one." She lifted her fingers. "That is the only provenance the founders asked for. Register the challenger."

The marshal's jaw worked. He stamped the papers. The small door-closing sound, this time, opened something instead.

c3_oru_warning.text:
Oru walked Rin a little apart from the line, Pae trailing wide-eyed at a respectful distance. Up close she smelled of old paper and cold tea, and she moved as though every joint had a long memory.

"They'll do it again," she said. "Not him — he is only a doorman with a pin. But the council behind him." She tilted her head toward the great inner doors, beyond which the roar lived. "Once there were many of us. Bond-Wardens, judges who could see whether a beast answers freely or is only obeying. Now there are a handful, and we are old, and the council that pays us has been bought by people who would rather the judging were a matter of provenance. Of money. Of who can afford the cleanest, coldest blade." Her clouded eyes found Rin's face. "Do you understand what I am telling you, challenger?"

"That I shouldn't have gotten in," Rin said.

"That you very nearly didn't, and that the reason you did is becoming a rare thing." Something fierce and tired flickered under the calm. "I have judged this Tournament for fifty years. I have waited a long while to feel a real bond come through that door. Faint as yours is — it is real." She paused. "Win or lose, do not let them tell you a bond is the weak blade. That lie is the whole game now. Remember that I told you otherwise."

Then she was gone, robes whispering, back into her side door. Rin stood holding their chipped blade in a cavern full of strangers, feeling smaller than ever and, for no reason they could name, a little less alone.

c3_coach_reunion.text:
The Coach was waiting where the registration hall opened onto the inner concourse, in the same gray coat he'd worn at the dish-hall, looking entirely unremarkable in a way that, Rin was beginning to suspect, took effort. He took one look at Rin's face and the freshly stamped papers and read the whole story without being told it.

"They tried to keep you out," he said. Not a question.

"A Warden kept me in."

Something passed behind his eyes — recognition, or memory. "Oru," he said softly, and let the name sit there a moment before he set it down. "Good. There's still one honest set of eyes on that council, then." He turned to walk Rin up the concourse, into the rising noise, and Pae fell in beside them like a duckling. "Listen to me now, because the gate is the easy part. Inside that ring there's a bracket, and the bracket has teeth."

choices.label: Lift your chin. You earned the stamp — walk in like you belong.
Keep your head down. Watch, learn the room, give nothing away.

c3_gate_proud.text:
Rin lifted their chin.

It was a small thing and it cost them more than the long climb had. They had spent a life making themself unnoticed — a tailings kid learns young that the safest shape is the one nobody looks at twice. But Oru had set two fingers on their blade and said real, and the marshal had stamped the papers, and Rin walked up the great concourse with their shoulders square and their chipped blade riding openly in their hand for anyone to see and sneer at.

Let them. The chip was theirs. The bond was theirs, faint and nameless and real. Rin had walked into a hundred rooms braced to be sent out of them, and just this once they walked in as if they meant to stay.

The Coach noticed. He said nothing, but the corner of his mouth moved, and he matched his pace to theirs instead of leading. Beside them Pae copied the chin-lift exactly, fierce and ridiculous, a child mimicking a courage they did not yet have to invent, and Rin felt the warmth of that catch in their chest and stay.

The concourse spilled them out into the lip of the Coliseum proper, and the world dropped away below. Tier on tier on tier of stone, ringed with banners, and at the bottom the dishes — a dozen great battle-dishes gleaming under the open sky, each one a polished bowl where a single blade could decide everything. The roar was a physical thing here, a tide. Rin stood at the rail with their head high and made themself look at all of it, the whole vast machine that had nearly turned them away, and did not look down. Not at the exits. Not this time.

c3_gate_quiet.text:
Rin kept their head down.

Not in shame — in survey. It was the oldest habit they had, older than the blade: walk into a new room small and quiet, give nothing away, and learn it before it can learn you. They kept their chipped blade close against their side and let their eyes do the work, reading the concourse the way the Coach had taught them to read a dish.

And there was so much to read. Crests Rin didn't recognize on coats that cost more than a year of dish-hall meals. Clusters of cold-eyed handlers in matching gray — Concord, by the cut of them, by the way the crowd parted to let them through. Spinners with blades cased in velvet, walking like they'd been promised the crown in the cradle. Rin filed each face, each posture, the way you file the position of the doors. Knowing the room was a kind of safety. It was, in fact, the only kind Rin had ever fully trusted.

The Coach watched them watch, and approved. "That's a spinner's eye," he murmured. "Half of every match is over before the launch. You read a room like someone who's had to." He didn't ask why. He never asked why; it was one of the things Rin trusted about him.

The concourse opened onto the lip of the Coliseum, the tiers falling away below to a dozen gleaming dishes under open sky, and Rin took it all in from beneath lowered lashes — vast, indifferent, dangerous — and felt the wobble in their chest go quiet under the cool weight of paying attention. Whatever this place was, they would understand it before it understood them.

c3_framing.text:
The Coach leaned on the rail beside Rin and looked down at the dishes the way a man looks at a country he used to live in.

"Single elimination," he said. "You lose once, you go home. To reach the crown you climb through the Gauntlet first — the open qualifier, the crush of every nobody who thinks they're a somebody. Survive that and you're in the Round of the Three Rivals." He held up a weathered hand and folded down a finger for each. "Kael. Fast, furious, a wolf-blade that bites before it thinks — and a boy underneath it who has never once been allowed to lose. Then Mira. Concord-trained, cold-precise; she'll have watched every match you've ever spun and solved you on paper before you launch. Then Brakk, in the semifinal — the largest spinner in the league and a storm-eagle to match. Beat all three and you reach the final."

He was quiet a moment.

"And in the final there is one figure no one has beaten. Not this year. Not in years. They call him the Masked Ace." The Coach's voice did not change, exactly, but something underneath it went careful, the way a floor goes careful over a weak board. "I won't lie to you, Rin. On skill alone you do not climb this. There are children down there who have trained since they could stand, with blades that cost more than your whole borough. Strength is not the thing that wins this Tournament."

"Then what is?" Rin asked.

The Coach almost answered. Rin watched him decide not to. "Come," he said instead. "There's something you should see before you believe me."

c3_raze_glimpse.text:
He led them down a ramp to a practice dish set apart from the others, walled on three sides, where a single figure spun alone.

The Masked Ace. He could only be that. He was perhaps Rin's age, slight, dressed in unrelieved gray, and his face was hidden behind a smooth pale mask with no expression worked into it at all — not fearsome, not proud, simply blank, a face that gave a watcher nothing to read. His blade turned in the center of the dish in a long, flawless, ringing spin, and he stood over it perfectly still, weaving the signs with hands that moved like clockwork. Listen. Steady. Turn. Faster than Rin had ever seen them woven, and cleaner, and emptier.

That was the wrongness. It took Rin a moment to find it. The signs were perfect and there was no joy in them. None at all. When Rin wove, even badly, there was a back-and-forth, a small living warmth, the blade answering like a friend who'd heard their name called. This was a person giving orders to a thing that had stopped arguing. And under it — Rin felt it before they understood it, a cold draft across the breastbone, a wrongness that lived in the chest and not the air — the blade's spin was beautiful and the beast inside it was not there. Not gone. Hiding. Flinching down so deep into the blur that Rin couldn't catch even a flicker of beast-shape.

Rin's own chipped blade, pocketed and still, gave one small cold shiver against their hip, as if it too had felt that draft and did not like it.

c3_coach_goes_still.text:
Rin turned to ask what they were seeing — and stopped.

The Coach had gone still. Not the listening stillness Rin knew, the one he sank into over a dish. This was the other kind, the kind a person goes when something long buried walks up and taps them on the shoulder. His eyes were on the masked spinner's hands, on the cold flawless weave, and his face had emptied of everything he usually kept arranged there. For one unguarded moment he looked old, and afraid, and grieved — and then he noticed Rin noticing, and the gray coat of his ordinariness came back down over it like a shutter.

"That," Rin said carefully, "is what I'd be up against."

"That is what the whole world is being taught to want," the Coach said. His voice was even again, but quieter. "A cleaner game. A colder one. They call it modern weaving. They sell it as strength." He watched the blade ring its flawless, joyless ring. "And every time a bonded spinner kneels to it on that floor, in front of all those people, it proves their argument for them. It says the old way was always weakness. It says a bond is something to be embarrassed by." He looked at Rin then, full on. "That is why you matter more than you know, and why a blade like yours frightens them more than a perfect one. You're carrying the thing they need everyone to forget."

Rin looked back down at the masked figure, the empty mask, the absent beast. They thought of Oru's clouded eyes and the word real, and of how alone the masked spinner stood in his walled-off dish, weaving perfectly to a thing that would not answer. Something in it was familiar — a boy standing exactly as alone as Rin had spent a life teaching themself to be. Rin filed it away with the Coach's shuttered face and the cold under-feeling, not yet knowing it was the most important thing they had seen all day.

c4_gauntlet_open.text:
The Gauntlet did not look like the Coliseum proper. It was a lesser ring tucked beneath the great stands, a dozen practice dishes ground into a stone floor that had felt ten thousand blades, and the light came down through a high slatted ceiling in long bars that caught the chalk in the air and made it hang there, slow and golden. Rin stood at the edge of dish four and breathed it in: hot metal, ground stone, the faint sweetness of rosin somebody had rubbed on a launcher cord. It smelled, almost exactly, like home.

The thought arrived before Rin could stop it, and Rin set it down again, gently, the way you set down something you are not allowed to keep.

Around the ring, the open qualifiers waited their turns — outer-borough kids in patched gear, a handful of guild cadets in pressed Concord grey, an old spinner with a blade worn to a nub of its old self. A marshal in a faded sash read names off a board nobody could see well, and a horn somewhere up in the true arena let out a long brass note that shook dust from the rafters. The real tournament, beginning above them. Down here was the gate you passed through to reach it.

Rin counted the exits without deciding to. Two stairwells, the marshal's arch, a service door wedged with a brick. It was an old habit and a useless one, because the only way out of the Gauntlet that mattered was forward, through every spinner in this room, into the bracket where three rivals and one masked finalist waited. Rin's hand found the chipped blade in their pocket — the no-name, the hand-me-down, the one thing that had never once been taken back — and the wobble in their chest went quiet, the way it only ever did with that small dead weight in their palm.
c4_gauntlet_open.title: The Gauntlet

c4_first_match.text:
"Dish four," the marshal called, and a name that was probably Rin's, mangled. "Against Toller, outer south."

The boy across the dish was broad and friendly and nervous, a quarry-town accent and a blade the color of river clay. He grinned at Rin, the open grin of someone who had not yet learned to be afraid of strangers, and Rin gave back the careful, pleasant half-smile they kept for exactly this — warm enough to be liked, light enough to leave nothing behind.

"First Gauntlet?" Toller asked.

"First everything," Rin said, which was true and gave away nothing.

They set their launchers. Rin's was scavenged like the blade, the ripcord frayed to a soft grey rope, and they notched the chipped blade into the prongs and felt the old familiar give. Across the way, Toller did the same, rushing it, his hands too eager.

The marshal lifted a hand. "Spinners ready. Three—"

Rin found Listen first, the easiest of the Six Signs, the one that was only attention. Somewhere under the chip and the scratches, the no-name beast turned over, a faint warmth like breath on the back of the neck.

"Two—"

Steady. Turn. The signs came clean now, after the Coach's months of patient drilling — all of them but the one Rin would not reach for.

"One. Spirits, fly!"

The cords ripped. Two blades hit the dish and screamed into their spin, and the small crowd around dish four leaned in, and Rin's whole careful world narrowed to a circle of stone and the bright ringing song of metal that did not yet know how it would end.

c4_unleash_lesson.text:
Toller fought the way nervous spinners always did — everything at once, all his weight forward. His clay blade lunged across the dish in a hard diagonal, and Rin read the line of it the way the Coach had taught, not with the eyes but with the blade: feeling the river-clay beast's intention arrive a half-beat before the steel did.

There were three ways to answer an attack like that. Rin knew them now the way they knew the four exits of a room.

You could unleash — pour your spirit-beast forward to meet force with greater force, a clean overwhelming charge. You could counter — let the other blade commit, read its pattern, and turn its own momentum into the thing that beat it. Or you could defend — circle, conserve, outlast, let a too-eager spin burn itself down to nothing.

Rin chose to unleash, because Toller deserved a clean fast match and not a long humiliating one. They wove Release — not the deep Release that called a true form, the Coach had been careful to say that was years and a named bond away — but the small honest Release that simply let the beast push. The no-name blade brightened, a pale shape blurring in its spin, and drove into the clay blade square-on.

The collision rang up through the floor. Toller's blade skipped, wobbled, and the bright ringing song of it changed pitch — that particular thin whine a spin makes when it is dying — and then it tipped, scraped a long grey arc across the stone, and lay still.

"Spirit's down," the marshal said. "Dish four to the challenger."

Toller blinked at his stopped blade, then up at Rin, and laughed, delighted and unhurt. "That was clean," he said. "That was really clean." Rin gave him the warm light smile and shook his offered hand and was already, somewhere behind their eyes, two exits ahead.

c4_pae_watches.text:
Pae was on the stairs where the marshals couldn't shoo them off, knees pulled up, watching with the whole of their small face. They had followed Rin to the capital the way a duckling follows the first thing it sees move, and Rin had said no, and Pae had come anyway, and Rin had not had the heart — had not, if they were honest, had the will — to send them back to the lower city alone.

"You unleashed," Pae said, breathless, when Rin came off the dish. "You could've just turned him aside, I saw it, you had the angle, but you unleashed. Why?"

It unsettled Rin, sometimes, how closely the kid watched. "Because he was nervous," Rin said. "A long match would've made it worse. Quick was kinder."

Pae stored this away like a coin. They had a wobbly beginner blade of their own, knotted to their wrist with a frayed launcher cord they'd tied themselves, and they spun it against the stair rail now in slow uneven loops, lips moving through the Six Signs Rin had shown them on the road. Listen. Steady. Turn.

"You'll teach me Release after," Pae said. It was not a question.

"After," Rin agreed, and meant it, and felt the small familiar pull of it — the way this kid had simply decided to belong to Rin and refused every gentle attempt to be set at a polite distance. Rin had spent fifteen years making themself easy to leave. Pae made it very hard to be left. It should have been a comfort. Mostly it felt like standing too close to a fire — the warmth and the worry of it arriving in the same breath, because everything Rin had ever let close enough to warm them had, eventually, gone.

c4_montage.text:
The morning narrowed into a rhythm, the way good things and hard things both do.

Dish six, against a girl with a hawk-quick copper blade who liked to feint. Rin let her commit and countered — read the false lunge for the lie it was, slid aside, and turned her own bright aggression into the thing that tipped her. She swore, then grinned, then asked Rin's name to remember it. Rin gave it and gave nothing else.

Dish two, against the old spinner with the worn-down blade, who fought patient and stubborn and refused to die. That one Rin won by defending — by circling, conserving, matching the old man's patience with a deeper one, until his ancient spin sighed out at last and he tipped his head in a respect that was almost a blessing. "You listen," the old man said. "Most of them only push. You listen." Rin thanked him and did not say that listening was just the safest way to stay one step ahead of being surprised.

Dish nine. Dish one. A blur of cords ripping and blades singing and the marshal's flat call — spirit's down, spirit's down, to the challenger. Rin won, and won, and won, and after each one shook the offered hand and traded the warm light words and walked away clean, taking nothing, leaving nothing, a friend to everyone for exactly as long as a match lasted.

Up on the stairs Pae kept a tally in chalk and beamed like the sun. And somewhere across the lesser ring, unhurried, a knot of pressed Concord grey had begun, Rin noticed, to watch dish four whenever the chipped no-name blade was on it — watching the way you watch something you mean to take the measure of.

c4_quiet_clue.text:
It was between matches, in the slow gold light, that Rin felt the thing they would spend the rest of the tournament trying not to understand.

They had crouched by the wall to check the chipped blade — habit, the way you check on a friend — turning it in their fingers, thumbing the old wound in its rim where some forgotten owner had cracked it against something harder than itself. And because no one was watching and there was no match to win, Rin did the thing they only ever did alone: they talked to it. Not words, exactly. Just attention, just the wordless steady press of company, the same thing they'd done at dawn in the lower-city hall for six years, the way you'd keep your hand on a sleeping animal so it knows you haven't gone.

And the beast answered.

Not loud. It never answered loud. But warmer than it had on any dish all morning — a slow turning-toward, a pressure like a held breath let halfway out, the faint blurred shape in the stilled blade seeming almost to lean into Rin's palm. It was stronger here, doing nothing, wanting nothing, than it had been in the heat of any win.

Rin's chest did the thing it was not supposed to do. Hope, that traitor flutter.

They closed their hand around the blade and made themself let the feeling go. The bond was broken; that was the settled fact of Rin's life. A truly bonded blade gave its spinner its name, and this one never had, not in six years, not once — and Rin had long ago decided what that silence meant. Nothing stays. Even this. Especially this. Better to know it now than to learn it the worse way, later, when it would cost more to lose.

c4_cadet_confront.text:
The Concord cadet found Pae first, which was its own kind of cruelty.

Rin came around the stairwell to the sound of it — a tall grey-pressed boy with a recruiter's polish already on him at sixteen, leaning over the small figure on the steps, plucking the wobbly beginner blade out of Pae's hands the way you'd take a stick from a dog. "This?" he was saying, turning it, laughing low to a friend. "They let tailings kids in with this now. Look at the cord — knotted it themselves. You can smell the lower city on it." Pae's face had gone tight and white, the particular blankness of a kid trying very hard not to cry in front of someone who'd enjoy it.

Rin was between them before they'd decided to move.

"That's not yours," Rin said, and took the wobbly blade out of the cadet's hand — not snatching, just removing it, the calm flat certainty of someone who had stood between smaller kids and bigger ones a hundred times in a hundred dish-halls. They pressed it back into Pae's grip and turned, putting their own body in the line of the cadet's sneer, an easy human wall.

The cadet looked Rin over and found the same patched gear, the same scavenged launcher. "Oh," he said, delighted. "There's two of you."

"There's two of us," Rin agreed mildly. "And you can go."

It was only later, walking Pae back to the stairs with the kid pressed warm against their side, that Rin noticed the shape of what they'd done — how fast and how completely they'd stepped in front of someone smaller, and how they would have done it for anyone, and how it had not once occurred to them to want anyone to do the same for them. They put themselves between Pae and the world without thinking. The thought of letting anyone stand between Rin and the world was not even a door they knew how to find.

c4_coach_aside.text:
The Coach was waiting by the wedged service door, half in shadow, the way he liked to be — a plain old man you would walk past a hundred times, which Rin had come to understand was a thing he had chosen rather than a thing he was.

"You shielded the little one," he said. Not a question.

"He had no business with Pae."

"No." The Coach watched the grey cadet rejoin his knot of Concord friends across the ring. "That one's last," he said. "They've arranged it. The marshal owes somebody a favor, and somebody wants the tailings kid to lose their last Gauntlet match to a cold-style cadet, in front of the grey coats, where it'll be seen." He said it without heat, the way he said most things, weight underneath and nothing on top.

Rin understood the shape of it from the Coliseum gate, from the things the Coach had let slip and the things he'd gone still over. "Cold style," Rin said. "The thing the winners use now."

"The thing the winners use now." The Coach turned the old dull blade he always carried over once in his palm — the silent one, the lightless one, the one he never spun and never explained — and put it away. "You'll feel it when he spins. Don't fight the feeling. Just notice it." His eyes found Rin's, pale and tired and, for one unguarded instant, frightened in a way Rin filed carefully away and did not ask about. "And Rin. You've won all morning by keeping everyone at the length of your arm. It's served you. Out there—" he tipped his head at the bracket waiting above them, the rivals, the masked thing at the top "—it won't be enough. Not because your blade is poor. Because that."

He didn't say what *that* was. He didn't have to. Rin felt it land anyway, in the place the hope had fluttered, and chose not to look at it.

c4_final_qualifier.text:
"Dish four," the marshal called, last of the morning, and the grey coats stopped pretending not to watch. "Against Cadet Vurn, Concord open."

Vurn was the recruiter-polished boy from the stairs, and he came to the dish without his earlier swagger — colder now, focused, a craftsman settling to work. His blade was a beautiful machined thing, edges bright, nothing scavenged or chipped anywhere on it, and he notched it into a launcher that gleamed. He did not grin at Rin. He did not look at Rin as a person at all, only as a problem with a known solution.

"Spinners ready," the marshal said.

Rin set the chipped blade in the frayed prongs of the scavenged launcher and found Listen, and the no-name beast turned toward them, warm, present, *here.* Across the dish, Vurn's hands moved through the readying sign, and something in the movement was wrong — the shapes were right and the feeling under them was inverted, a sign turned from a question into a command. Rin's skin prickled with a cold that had nothing to do with the air.

"Three—"

The cold under-feeling. The thing the Coach had said to notice and not fight. Rin noticed it now, a low wrong hum beneath the dish like a note played a half-tone flat, and somewhere inside the gleaming machined blade something living *flinched.*

"Two. One. Spirits, fly!"

The cords tore. Two blades hit the stone — one warm and chipped and humming, one bright and cold and faintly, terribly afraid of its own spinner — and the Gauntlet's last match screamed open under the gold and the watching grey.

choices.label: Unleash — meet the cold surge head-on and overwhelm it.
Counter — let the cold blade overcommit, then turn it against itself.
Defend — circle and outlast; a forced spin burns itself out.

c4_unleash_branch.text:
Rin chose to unleash, because there was something in the cold wrong hum of Vurn's blade that Rin did not want to dance with one beat longer than they had to. Meet it. End it. Get the living thing inside that gleaming steel away from the boy who was hurting it.

Rin wove Release — the small honest push — and asked, did not command, *now, with me,* and the no-name beast answered with a warmth that surprised even Rin. The chipped blade brightened, the pale shape in its blur surging, and drove straight into the heart of the cold blade's charge.

The collision was not like the others that morning. Where Toller's clay blade had simply rung, Vurn's machined steel met Rin's and *recoiled* — and Rin felt, through the contact, the difference between the two beasts laid bare. Theirs pushed because Rin had asked and it had chosen to. Vurn's pushed because it was afraid not to. One was a duet. The other was a leash.

The leashed beast broke first. Not the blade — the bond. Rin felt it through the steel, the instant the cold sign's grip slipped and the frightened thing inside Vurn's blade simply stopped answering him at all, going flat and obedient and dead-quiet in the same breath. The gleaming blade's spin sheared sideways, lurched, and toppled, ringing that thin dying whine across the stone.

"Spirit's down," the marshal said, into a silence the grey coats had not expected. "Dish four to the challenger."

Rin stood over the two stopped blades, breathing hard, and did not feel the clean bright thing they'd felt all morning. They felt the cold place where Vurn's beast had flinched and gone silent, and understood, in their own body, why the Coach said the word *taboo* the way other people said the word *grief.*

c4_counter_branch.text:
Rin chose to counter, because the cold blade was fast and forced and furious, and the surest way to beat a thing that pushes too hard is to let it.

Rin gave ground. Wove Turn and circled, light, reading the gleaming blade's line the way they'd read every blade all morning — except this one was easier and worse to read, because there was no living instinct in its aggression, only Vurn's will driving a frightened thing where it did not want to go. The cold sign made the blade fast but stupid. It went exactly where it was told, and what it was told was: forward, forward, harder, *win.*

So Rin let it have forward. Slid aside at the last instant, the chipped blade kissing the cold one's flank and adding the smallest nudge to its overcommitted charge — and the machined blade, with nothing in it that could feel a trap coming, hurtled past the point of its own balance.

Rin felt the bond slip at the exact moment the spin did. The frightened thing inside Vurn's blade, asked for the impossible and punished for failing, simply let go — flinched all the way out and went flat and silent — and the gleaming steel, suddenly riderless, wobbled, scraped a long bright arc across the stone, and lay down.

"Spirit's down," the marshal said. "Dish four to the challenger."

The grey coats were quiet. Vurn stared at his stopped, beautiful, dead-quiet blade with an expression Rin recognized — not the sting of losing, but the deeper confusion of a tool that had failed him, with no idea that the tool had been alive, and afraid, and that he had been the thing it was most afraid of. Rin looked at the cold blade and felt no triumph at all, only the cold place where its beast had cringed away, and filed it next to everything the Coach had refused to explain.

c4_defend_branch.text:
Rin chose to defend, because the cold sign had made Vurn's blade fast and bright and brutal — and a forced thing, the Coach had taught, burns hotter and dies sooner than a thing that spins because it wants to.

So Rin did not meet the cold charge. Rin survived it. Wove Steady and circled the dish's edge, conserving the chipped blade's patient spin, letting Vurn throw blow after gleaming blow that found only the place Rin's blade had just been. It cost something to take that punishment and give nothing back — every cold strike sent a wrong hum up through the floor, that low half-flat note, and each time it landed Rin felt the living thing inside Vurn's steel flinch on its own behalf, recoiling from the very violence its spinner forced it to do.

Vurn pushed harder, because cold spinners only know how to push harder. And the brighter his blade burned, the faster it spent itself — a fire that scorches has nothing left to warm. Rin watched the gleaming spin begin to thin, watched the cold sign demand more and more from a beast with less and less to give, until the machined blade's furious song climbed up and up into that thin dying whine.

Then, all at once, it had nothing left. The cold-driven spin guttered, the frightened beast inside it finally simply *stopped,* and the beautiful blade tipped, scraped, and went still — undone not by Rin's strength but by the cruelty of its own spinner, who had spent it like a coin.

"Spirit's down," the marshal said. "Dish four to the challenger."

Rin's blade was still turning, warm and unhurried, when they crouched to lift it. They did not look at Vurn. They looked at the silent cold blade and thought: *that's what it does. It wins and wins and the thing inside goes quiet.* And was, for the first time, afraid of the top of the bracket.

c4_qualified.text:
The marshal scratched a mark beside Rin's mangled name on the board nobody could read. "Challenger qualifies," he said, bored, official, and it was done — Rin was through the Gauntlet and into the Round of the Three Rivals, and the words should have felt enormous and instead felt very quiet, the way the most important things sometimes do.

Pae reached them first, barreling off the stairs, chalk tally forgotten, wrapping skinny arms around Rin's middle before Rin could compose the polite gentle distance they kept ready. "You're in," Pae said into Rin's coat. "You're *in,* I saw all of it, you didn't even—" and then ran out of words and just held on, and Rin let them, one hand awkward in the kid's hair, the warmth and the worry arriving together as they always did.

The Coach came across slower. He looked at Rin a long moment, and the thing in his pale face was unmistakable and rare — pride, plain and warm, the pride of a man who had decided long ago to stop hoping for things and had been ambushed by hope anyway. "Clean," he said, which from him was a speech.

Then his gaze dropped to the chipped blade in Rin's palm — to the old crack in its rim, the worn no-name steel, the frayed cord — and something else crossed his face that he tried to put away before Rin could see, and didn't quite. Worry. The careful arithmetic of a man wondering whether a scavenged blade that had survived a morning of nervous quarry kids could survive Kael, and Mira, and Brakk, and the cold thing waiting at the very top.

"Rest it tonight," was all he said, nodding at the blade. "It's carried you further than anyone gave it a right to." He did not say *and it has so much further still to carry you.* But Rin, who had spent a lifetime reading the things people didn't say, heard it anyway, and closed their hand around the warm chipped steel, and turned to face the bracket.

c5_into_the_round.text:
The Gauntlet was behind them now, and that was the strange part. Rin kept waiting to feel it leave — the way a held breath leaves, all at once, in a rush — but it didn't. The dust of the open qualifier still clung to their sleeves. The chipped blade still sat in the loop at their hip, warm from the last match, its no-name core humming the low, private hum that only Rin had ever heard. And the Coach walked half a pace ahead, saying nothing, which from him was a kind of saying everything.

The Rivals Round was held in the inner arena, a deeper bowl than the qualifier pits, ringed with tiered stone that climbed up and up until the spectators near the rim were no bigger than chalk marks. The light came down filtered and gray through a high vaulted opening, and it smelled of hot metal and old rope and the sweat of people who had wanted something very badly for a very long time. Rin counted the exits without meaning to. Three at the floor, two on the mezzanine, one that was probably a service door. The habit was older than the tournament, older than the Coach, older than almost everything except the blade.

"Three of them stand between you and the final," the Coach had told them at the gate, in the plain weighted way he said important things. "Win all three and you face the one nobody beats." He had not looked at Rin when he said it. He had looked at the chipped blade, and his face had done the small unreadable thing it did, the thing Rin had learned to file away and not ask about.

Now a gate-marshal called a name across the floor, and the name was Rin's, and the wobble in their chest started up like a top wound too tight.
c5_into_the_round.title: Kael, the Cocky Qualifier

c5_kael_entrance.text:
He came in like he owned the building and was thinking about selling it.

The boy across the dish was maybe a year older than Rin, lean and quick-looking, with a launcher slung over one shoulder in a way that was meant to be careless and was instead very, very practiced. He wore his club's colors — an outer-borough crest Rin half-recognized, a struggling little house from the wrong side of Coilspire — but he wore them the way you'd wear a crown you'd decided to pretend was nothing. Silver cord wrapped his wrist. His grin arrived before he did.

"So you're the tailings kid everyone's whispering about." His voice carried, pitched to reach the lower tiers, where a thin scatter of spectators leaned in. "The one who scavenged their way up the Gauntlet on a blade somebody threw out." He let that land, tipped his head, made it a compliment and an insult in the same breath. "Relax. This won't take long. I'll make it quick, and you can tell people you went two rounds with Kael of the Ironreach before he sent you home."

Rin said nothing. That was usually the right move — let the loud ones fill the silence; they always did — and Kael obliged, spinning his blade up into his palm and catching it, spinning it up again, a little nervous engine that wouldn't sit still.

But Rin was watching his eyes, not his mouth. The mouth was a performance. The eyes kept flicking, fast, to the high tier on the arena's shaded side, where three figures in pale Concord coats sat with the stillness of people taking notes. Scouts. Every time Kael glanced up there, the grin tightened at one corner, just slightly, like a screw being turned a half-thread too far.

Rin knew that look. They had worn that look. It was the look of someone certain they were about to be left behind.

c5_greywind_lore.text:
Kael set his blade to the launcher for show, just to let Rin see it, and the spirit in it answered before the cord was even drawn.

It rose off the silver core as a smear of motion, a long low shape the eye couldn't quite hold — and then for half a heartbeat it sharpened into something with a lean back and a dropped head and a hunger in the set of its shoulders. A wolf. Not the storybook kind that ran in a warm dark mass under the moon, but the other kind: the one bred apart and kept apart, taught that the pack was a story for weaker animals, taught to win alone because winning was the only thing that earned it a place to sleep. Greywind, the murmur went up from the spectators who knew the bracket. Kael's wolf. The fastest, most merciless blade in the outer boroughs.

Rin felt it before they understood it. The wolf-spirit leaned forward, always forward, all attack and no guard, the way a thing leans when it has learned that stopping is the same as losing and losing is the same as being put outside in the cold. It over-reached because Kael over-reached. It snapped at everything because Kael had never, not once, been allowed to simply stand still and be enough.

A blade is a two-way mirror, the Coach liked to say. Rin had nodded at the time the way you nod at a thing you don't yet believe. They believed it now, watching the silver wolf strain at the air. The boy and the beast were the same animal wearing two skins. Both of them fast. Both of them frightened.
