Both of them sure, down in the marrow, that the moment they were found wanting was the moment the world would let them go.

The chipped blade at Rin's hip hummed, low and warm, as if it had recognized a cousin.

c5_rin_reads_him.text:
It was a strange gift, and Rin had never asked for it: they could read the fear of being left in almost anyone. They could read it in the line of a shoulder, in the half-beat too long someone held a smile, in the way a person's eyes went to the door of a room they had only just entered. They had been reading it their whole life — first to know when an adoption was souring, when the warmth in a foster house was cooling toward the polite distance that always, always came before the bag was packed. Reading other people's fear was how Rin had survived their own. Get out before you're put out. Count the exits. Need nothing.

So they saw Kael clearly, the way you can only see a wound that matches your own. The swagger was a jacket thrown over something cold. The 'this won't take long' was a boy talking fast so that no one — least of all the pale coats in the high tier — would notice the part of him that was certain he was about to lose, and that losing would prove the thing he had been raised to fear: that he was not, had never been, would never be, quite good enough to keep.

The odd thing, the thing Rin would not have been able to say out loud, was this: they could see the fear of being left in everyone they ever met. Everyone except themselves. Their own they kept folded so small and so deep that it had stopped looking like fear at all. It looked, from the inside, like wisdom. It looked like simply knowing better than to want.

Kael caught them looking. The grin flickered. "What," he said, sharper now, lower, just for Rin. "You feeling sorry for me? Don't. People who feel sorry for me lose."

There was a whole life in that sentence. Rin heard it. The referee raised a hand for the readying. One breath, now, to decide how to meet him.

c5_approach_choice.text:
Kael's blade hung ready in his hand. The scouts watched from the shaded tier. The whole arena had narrowed to the space between two children who had each, in their own way, already decided no one was coming to stay.

Rin could feel the choice in their chest like a second pulse. Meet him soft, or meet him bright. Both were true. Both were Rin.

choices.label: Smile, and offer him a fair, friendly match.
Meet his confidence with confidence of your own.

c5_calm_branch.text:
Rin let the silence go, and then they did the thing no one ever did to Kael. They smiled. Not the thin, defensive smile of the lower city, the one that gave nothing away — a real one, small and steady and entirely unafraid.

"You're fast," Rin said. Their voice didn't carry the way Kael's did; it didn't have to. It went straight across the dish to him alone, low and even. "Fastest I've seen. I watched your Gauntlet runs." That last part was true, and Kael's grin slipped a notch at the truth of it, because a compliment he could deflect but the fact that this nobody had studied him, had thought he was worth studying, landed somewhere he had no armor for. "So let's have a good match. A clean one. You bring everything you've got, I'll bring everything I've got, and whoever's left spinning earns it. Deal?"

For a moment Kael just stared. Whatever he had braced for — sneering, fear, the brittle bravado he knew how to break — this was not it. His mouth opened. Closed. The glance he threw up at the scouts was different this time; not a check, but almost a flinch, as if he'd briefly forgotten they were there.

"You don't get it," he said, quieter, and the performance had thinned enough that Rin could hear the real boy underneath, the one who had never in his life been offered a thing without a hook in it. "Nobody just — wants a good match. Everybody wants a win. You're supposed to want to crush me."

"I want to spin against you," Rin said simply. "That's a different thing."

Something moved behind Kael's eyes — confusion, mostly, and under the confusion a thin, unwilling thread of something that looked almost like relief. He set his jaw and lifted his blade, and when he answered, the swagger was back, but it was thinner now, more honest. "Fine. Fair match. Don't blame me when fair gets you launched out of the dish."

But he was smiling when he said it, and for the first time, it reached his eyes.

c5_bold_branch.text:
Rin lifted their chin and let Kael see it land — not the wound, the steel. They stepped up to the line so that the toes of their worn boots nearly touched the rim of the dish, and they held his gaze until the loud silver boy was the one who had to keep talking to fill the quiet.

"Quick, then," Rin said, and their voice came out lower than Kael's, but it carried farther, because it wasn't performing for the tiers; it was only for him. "You keep saying it. Quick, won't take long, send me home. So stop telling me and show me." A beat. The corner of Rin's mouth curled. "Unless the talking is the part you're good at."

A ripple went through the lower tiers — an oh — and Kael's grin froze, then cracked wide into something fiercer and far more alive than the bored sneer he'd walked in with. He laughed, one sharp bark, and the sound had real delight in it, the delight of a boy who had been braced for pity or fear and gotten neither.

"Oh," he said, rolling his shoulder, the launcher coming up smooth and fast. "Oh, the scrap-blade's got teeth. Good. Good. I was worried this was going to be sad." He flashed another glance at the pale coats in the high tier, but for once the glance wasn't a flinch — it was a flourish, a here, watch this. Rin had handed him the one thing his father's house had never let him have: an opponent who'd treat the fight as worth his whole self, no quarter asked, none given.

"Don't blink," Kael said, and the silver wolf surged up off his core, lean and hungry and matching its master breath for breath.

"You first," Rin answered.

The heat between them was a real thing now, bright and clean, two fires daring each other higher. It was the closest thing to fun Rin had felt since the dish-halls at dawn.

c5_readying.text:
The referee stepped to the rim and lifted both hands, and the arena drew its breath.

Rin set the chipped blade to the launcher. Their fingers found the worn places in the grip by memory, the chip in the rim that had been there longer than they could remember, the faint hum that rose to meet their palm like something turning over in its sleep. They did not reach for OPEN. They never reached for OPEN in front of a crowd; the sign that asked to be known was the one sign that, every time they tried it, made the core go flat and quiet and ashamed. Instead they wove the readying — Listen first, the way the Coach had taught, the way you'd lean toward a friend mid-sentence to catch the next word. The blade leaned back. Steady, then, the two of them finding the same center of weight, the boy and the no-name beast and the cord Pae had tied for luck all settling into one held line.

Across the dish, Kael wove his own readying, and his was all forward motion, no Listen at all that Rin could see — the wolf already straining, already half-launched in spirit before the cord was pulled. He fights to outrun the quiet moment, Rin thought, and was almost sad about it, and pushed the sadness down where it wouldn't slow their hands.

The referee's voice rang out over the silent bowl, old as the tournament, old as the first cooled spark.

"Spinners. On my count."

Up in the shaded tier, the pale coats leaned in. Somewhere far above, the Coach stood very still. And the wobble in Rin's chest, for one suspended instant, went quiet — the way it only ever did right here, right at the edge of the spin, with a blade in their hand and something waiting to turn alongside them.

c5_launch.text:
"Three."

The word dropped into the silence like a stone into a still well. Rin's whole body went taut over the launcher, weight forward, eyes on the dish and not on Kael, because the Coach had drilled it into them a hundred times — you do not spin against a person, you spin against the truth of the dish, and the person is only the weather. The chipped core warmed under their hand, that low hum climbing, brightening, the no-name beast gathering itself the way a sleeper gathers toward waking without quite breaking the surface.

"Two."

Across from them, Kael bared his teeth in something that was equal parts grin and snarl, the silver wolf coiled and shivering with the need to be loosed. Whatever had passed between them at the line — the fair word or the fierce one — it had changed the air. This was no longer a prodigy crushing a scrap-blade kid for the watching scouts. This was two of the same wounded animal, finally, gloriously, met.

"One."

Rin breathed out. Everything they were narrowed to the cord beneath two fingers, to the chip in the rim, to the warm faithful hum of the only thing in the whole turning world that had never once left them. Whatever happened in the next sixty seconds, this part was true. This part had always been true.

The referee's hand fell, and the cry went up — the oldest cry there was, the one every child in the Spun World learned before they learned to read, the one that called the sparks of the First Spin down out of the blur and into the bright spinning now.

"Spirits, fly!"

And the blades flew.

c6_launch.text:
The count fell away into nothing, and then the blades were in the air.

Rin felt the ripcord tear free of their fist, felt the old chipped blade leave their hand the way a held breath leaves the chest, and for one suspended instant the whole arena tipped sideways into silence. Then the dish caught both blades at once and the sound came rushing back — the flat ringing whir of two spins finding the same bowl of polished stone, the crowd's low roar pressing down from the tiers like weather.

Across the dish, Greywind hit the rim and ran.

That was the only word for it. Kael's silver wolf-blade did not settle into a careful orbit the way the qualifier blades had; it bolted, low and hungry, carving a hard line straight for Rin's center. In the blur above its crown Rin caught the shape of the thing that lived inside it — a long grey body, ears flat, all forward motion and no doubt — and felt, under their own ribs, the answering jolt of something that had decided long ago that the safest place to be was already attacking.

Rin's blade wobbled.

Not badly. Not yet. But the chip in its rim caught the spin wrong on the turn, the way it always did under pressure, a faint sick stutter that no one else in the stadium could possibly have heard and that Rin heard the way you hear your own name. Hold, they thought, not a sign yet, just a wish. Hold together. The blade steadied. The wolf came on. And somewhere far down beneath the noise, the no-name beast turned over once, listening, and waited to be told what they were.
c6_launch.title: Wolf and the Wobble

c6_first_exchange.text:
Kael was talking. Of course he was talking.

"You feel that?" he called across the dish, grinning, both hands still raised from the launch as though he might conduct the match like music. "That's the part where it starts to get away from you."

Greywind clipped the edge of Rin's orbit — a glancing blow, testing, the contact sparking a thin shriek of metal — and spun off without committing, circling back wide. Fast. The wolf was so fast that watching it made the breath go shallow, and Rin understood at once that Kael had not been bluffing in the ring beforehand. The swagger was real. It was just not the whole of him.

Because Rin was watching his face, the way they watched every face — out of an old habit of reading a room for the exact moment it decided it was done with you — and they saw the thing the grin was built over. Each time Greywind struck and pulled back without finishing, a flicker crossed Kael that he wiped away too fast: not triumph. A quick checking glance toward the stands, toward the cool grey row where the Concord scouts sat with their tablets and made their small unbothered notes. He was not spinning to beat Rin. He was spinning so that the people who graded him would not, this time, find him wanting.

Rin knew that exact arithmetic. Had run it themselves a hundred mornings. Win so they can't send you back.

Greywind wheeled and came again, harder, and the dish trembled under the wolf's hunger, and the moment to choose what kind of fight this was going to be arrived all at once.

choices.label: Unleash your spirit-beast — meet the wolf head-on
Read his pattern, then counter
Defend, and outlast him

c6_br_unleash.text:
Rin stopped holding back.

There was a kind of permission in it, a loosening — the same thing Kael had been chasing all match, except Rin did not reach for it to be seen. They reached for it because the wolf was lonely and going too fast and someone in this dish ought to answer that with their whole self instead of half. Listen. Turn. Rin let the no-name beast come up to the surface of the spin, no longer a shape hinted at in the blur but a presence leaning forward into it, and the chipped blade brightened on the dish like a coal breathed on.

Greywind committed. It always would. Kael flung both hands wide and the wolf dove for the kill — and Rin, instead of slipping aside, turned straight into the charge and accelerated.

The blades met at the dead center of the dish with a crack that flattened the crowd's roar to nothing. For a heartbeat the two spins locked, screaming, rim grinding rim, the chip in Rin's blade shrieking its protest — and then the no-name beast pushed, not harder than the wolf but more whole than the wolf, all of itself against all of Greywind's hunger, and the silver blade skipped.

Just a skip. A stumble in a perfect spin. But Greywind's line broke, and the wolf staggered wide, and Kael's grin slipped clean off his face for the first time. Rin felt the beast inside their own blade flare warm — not with the cold satisfaction of winning, but with something closer to recognition, as though it had finally been allowed to mean what it did.

c6_br_counter.text:
Rin let the wolf come.

Not passively — there was nothing passive in it — but with the whole of their attention narrowed to a single question they had been asking since the launch: where does he always go? Because Kael did have a pattern, the way frightened people always have a pattern, a thing they do when the quiet moment threatens, and Rin had been collecting it exchange by exchange. Greywind never circled left. It feinted, it pulled back, it bolted — but every true commitment came from the right, low and inside, the angle of a boy who had learned to attack before anyone could decide he wasn't worth keeping.

Steady, Rin thought, and held their orbit loose and slow and stupid-looking, an invitation, the open flank Kael could not refuse.

He didn't.

Greywind dove from the right, low and inside, exactly on its line — and Rin was already turning, had been turning before the wolf moved, so that the killing charge met not Rin's center but the curved hard shoulder of a blade angled to send it skating off down the dish wall. The contact rang like a struck bell. Greywind shot wide, fighting for its line, spin scattered, and Kael made a sound that was almost a laugh of pure surprise.

"You were waiting for that," he said, half-accusing, half-delighted.

Rin didn't answer. The no-name beast had gone bright and steady under their attention — and Rin felt, with a small private shock, that it was not the read that had warmed it. It was that they had spent the whole match looking at Kael instead of past him.

c6_br_defend.text:
Rin gave the center away.

It went against everything the crowd wanted — you could feel them want the clash, the spectacle, two blades hurling themselves at each other — but Rin had spent a childhood being the one who outlasted, the one still standing in the dish-hall when the others had spent themselves and gone home, and they knew a truth about hunger that Kael did not yet know: it burns fast.

So Rin ceded ground. Hold. They drew the chipped blade out to the wide rim and let it ride the long quiet edge of the dish, conserving every turn, while Greywind raged at the empty center looking for something to break. The wolf struck and struck. Each blow Rin met at a glancing angle, bleeding the force off sideways, never standing to trade — let it skid, let it ring, let it cost Kael a little more spin than it cost Rin each time.

"Stand and fight," Kael snapped, and there it was, the fear leaking through the grin — because a boy who has been taught that winning fast is the only kind of winning that counts cannot bear a fight that refuses to end. "Come on. Stand and fight me."

Rin held the rim.

And Greywind began, by slow degrees, to slow. The hunger that made it so deadly was the same hunger that spent it; its line wavered, its howl in the blur thinned. The no-name beast, by contrast, hummed low and even under Rin's hand, warming as it went — content, Rin realized, not because they were winning, but because for once they had not flinched at being needed for the long haul.

c6_the_finish.text:
After that, the end came quickly, the way ends do once a spin's heart has gone out of it.

Greywind wobbled — that small, fatal stutter Rin knew so intimately from the other side — and then its proud line collapsed into a stagger, and the silver wolf-blade tipped, scraped, and lay down dead at the bottom of the dish with a sound like a coin settling. Rin's chipped blade spun on above it, scarred and brightly alive, slowing now too but still turning, still theirs.

The referee's arm came up. Somewhere a horn sounded. The roar of the crowd broke over the dish like a wave finally allowed to fall.

But Rin was not watching the referee. Rin was watching Kael.

Because this was the part Rin had braced for all their life — the part where the person you have just bested decides what to do with the fact of you. They had seen it go a hundred ways in the dish-halls: the cold shoulder, the muttered excuse, the sudden discovery that you were never really friends to begin with. Kael had everything riding on this match and a row of grey scouts who had just watched him lose, and his face had gone very still and very young, the grin nowhere now, the mask off entirely.

He's going to make it ugly, Rin thought, and was already, out of pure old reflex, counting the exits — the tunnel mouth, the competitors' gate, the gap in the rail.

Kael bent down, picked his dead wolf-blade up off the dish floor, turned it over once in his hands, and looked at it. Then he looked at Rin. And Rin watched him brace for something too.

c6_kael_turn.text:
What Kael was bracing for, Rin realized, was to be mocked.

It was written all over him — the flinch held ready behind the eyes, the shoulders drawn up against a blow he was certain was coming, because in the world that built Kael a loss was not a thing that happened to you, it was a thing you became, and the only question left was how loudly the winner would say it. He had lost in front of the scouts. He had lost to a no-name tailings kid with a chipped hand-me-down blade. He was waiting, with the awful patience of someone who has done this before, for Rin to twist the knife.

Rin knew that wait. Rin had invented that wait.

So they did the only thing they knew how to do with it, which was to refuse it. "Greywind's faster than anything I've ever spun against," Rin said, and meant it, and let it be simple. "You nearly had me twice. The second time I just got lucky on the read."

Kael stared at them.

For a long moment nothing happened, and Rin thought they had got it wrong — and then something in Kael's face came apart, not into hurt but into pure startled relief, and the boy who had never once been told he had done well, who had been waiting his whole life to be found wanting and finally hung out to dry, laughed.

It was a real laugh, loud and undignified and a little wet at the edges, and it rang up into the tiers. "Lucky," he repeated, shaking his head, grinning that grin for real now. He crossed the dish and stuck out his hand. "Nobody's that lucky. Kael. You're going to have to let me buy you something terrible to eat."

c6_the_clasp.text:
Rin looked at the offered hand.

It was a small thing, a hand across a dish, the most ordinary gesture in the sport. People did it after every match. It meant nothing. It meant everything. Rin's whole body did the thing it always did when someone got within reach — the quiet inventory, the held breath, the part of them already rehearsing how this would end so the ending could not catch them off guard. Friendship at arm's length was safe. Rin was very good at arm's length. They could shake the hand and say something light and let Kael drift back into the bracket as one more opponent-shaped acquaintance, and nothing would ever be able to hurt.

Down in the chipped blade, slowing on the dish, the no-name beast stirred.

Rin felt it the way you feel warmth come back into a cold hand — a low, unhurried brightening, and it was not coming from the win. The win was already old. It was coming from now, from this, from the hand held out in the open air between two people who had nothing to gain from each other anymore. The beast had been quiet through the whole victory. It woke for the friendship.

Rin took the hand.

Kael hauled them up out of their crouch with a grip far too strong, still laughing, already talking — "You spin like an old person, you know that? All patient. Drives me insane" — and the contact was warm and real and Rin did not let go right away, and the wobble in their chest, the one that had been there as long as they could remember, went, for just a moment, perfectly still.

c6_kaels_corner.text:
Kael did not drift back into the bracket.

Kael attached himself, instantly and totally, the way only a person starved of belonging can attach to the first one who feeds them. He walked Rin off the dish with an arm slung over their shoulders he had not asked permission to sling, narrating the match back to the whole tunnel as though Rin had not been there for it — "and then, and THEN, this absolute menace just sits on the rim like they're waiting for a bus" — to anyone who would listen and several people who would not. The grey scouts had already gone. Kael did not look at where they had been. It was, Rin noticed, the first time all day his eyes had not gone to that row.

At the mouth of the competitors' tunnel he finally stopped, and some of the noise went out of him, and he said, more quietly, "You're in the next round." It was not quite a question. "So am I. On the other side of the bracket." He turned the dead wolf-blade over in his hands. "Walk over with me? They post the new pairings at the east gate. I hate reading those things alone."

And there it was again — the small open door, the chance to keep things easy, to say I'll catch up and slip back into the safe solitude Rin had carried like a coat their whole life. The reflex came up fast and familiar. No, thanks. I'm fine on my own.

Rin looked at Kael, who hated reading the pairings alone, and recognized the lie in I'm fine on my own because they had been telling it longer than Kael had.

"Yeah," Rin said. "Okay. Let's walk."

Kael lit up like it was nothing. To him, maybe it was. To Rin it was the second hand they had taken in an hour, and the chipped blade in their pocket was still warm.

c6_the_seed.text:
The pairings board at the east gate was a great lacquered thing with the bracket inked across it, and they read it shoulder to shoulder while the crowd thinned around them and the lamps came up against the falling light.

"Mira next, for you," Kael said, tapping a name in the column. "The Concord one. She's terrifying. Reads you like a book you didn't know you'd written." He pulled a face. "Then me, if I get through Brakk, which — big if. You've seen Brakk?" He spread his arms as far as they would go, which was not far enough, and gave up. "Bigger than that."

Rin barely heard. Their eye had snagged on the far right of the board, on the single name that sat alone above the final, with no club beside it and no club behind it: the Masked Ace.

Kael followed their gaze and his voice changed — dropped, lost the performance. "Yeah. Him." He glanced around, then leaned in. "You want to hear something strange? There was a Concord recruiter circling him this morning. Before the round. Practically bowing." He frowned at the name as though it might frown back. "Which makes no sense, because nobody — and I mean nobody — has ever seen that guy's beast. He's spun a dozen matches in this Tournament and not one person can tell you what's inside his blade. You don't recruit a bonded spinner you've never seen bond."

A cold thread of under-feeling crawled up Rin's spine — the same wrongness they'd felt watching Raze warm up at the gate, that flinch in the air with no source. They did not have a word for it yet.

"Maybe there's nothing to see," Rin said quietly.

Kael laughed, uneasy. "Now that," he said, "is a horrible thought. Come on. I'm starving and you owe me terrible food." And he steered them off toward the lights of the competitors' quarter, talking the whole way, and Rin let themself be steered.

c7_hall_at_night.text:
The competitors' hall emptied slowly after the day's matches, the way a tide goes out — first the crowds, then the officials, then the spinners themselves, until the great vaulted room held only the night-lamps and the smell of cooling metal. Rin had learned long ago that the safest hours were the ones nobody else wanted. They sat on a low bench against the far wall, where the lamplight thinned to grey and a person could see the whole length of the hall, every door, every shadow that might move.

The habit was older than memory. Count the exits. Mark the faces. Know, always, how to leave before being left.

Tonight there were four doors, and Rin had counted them twice before they noticed they were doing it.

The chipped blade rested in their open palm, dead-quiet now, its battered rim catching a sliver of lamp-glow. Earlier, in the practice dish, it had spun warmer than it had in weeks — that small, faint answering hum that Rin had never been able to explain to anyone and had never tried. They had won today. They had a name in the bracket now, a wolf-blade boy in their corner, a younger kid sleeping somewhere down the corridor. By every measure that mattered, the lower-city orphan had climbed further than anyone expected.

So Rin could not say why the wobble in their chest would not go quiet.

It was the strange ache of getting what you wanted. Of having something now that could, therefore, be taken. Rin turned the blade over and watched the chip in its edge catch the light, and waited, as they always did, for the room to grow still enough to feel safe in.
c7_hall_at_night.title: Between Rounds

c7_kael_arrives.text:
Boots scuffed the floor — loud, unhurried, the gait of someone who had never in his life worried about being heard. Rin knew it was Kael before they looked up.

He dropped onto the bench beside them without asking, the way he did everything, and for a moment said nothing at all, which was so unlike him that Rin glanced sideways to check he was still breathing.

The swagger was off. That was the thing Rin noticed first, the way they noticed everything: the small adjustments people made when they thought no one was watching. In the ring Kael wore his confidence like a borrowed jacket, two sizes too bold, every motion announcing itself. Here, at the dead end of the day, the jacket was off. His shoulders had come down. He looked, suddenly, exactly fifteen.

"Couldn't sleep," he said, before Rin could ask. "Greywind gets restless after a match. Keeps me up." He turned his own silver blade over in his fingers, and Rin understood that the wolf was not the one keeping him awake.

"I count exits," Rin offered. It surprised them, saying it. "When I can't sleep. I count the doors."

Kael snorted. "That's grim."

"It is."

He looked at them then, really looked, and something in his face shifted — recognition, maybe, the way one animal knows another's wariness without being told its cause. Then he looked away, out at the long empty hall, and his thumb worried at the edge of his blade, around and around, and Rin recognized that too. A motion to outrun a quiet you didn't want to sit inside.

c7_kael_father.text:
"My father's coming to the semifinals," Kael said. He said it the way you'd report bad weather. "Assuming I make it that far. He's never watched me spin in person. Not once."

Rin held still. They had learned that the surest way to make someone close back up was to lean toward the opening too fast.

"Blade-house," Kael went on, when Rin only waited. "You've heard of us, probably. Everyone has. Three generations of champions and a wall of crowns and a father who reviews you like a ledger." His mouth twisted around the next part. "You know what he's never said to me? Not once, in fifteen years? Well done. Not after a win, not after anything. There's always a flaw to fix. Always the next thing I should've done cleaner."

The thumb went around and around the blade's edge.

"So you learn to never stop," he said. "You learn that the second you stand still, that's when he finds you wanting. Greywind fights like that because I fight like that. We don't know how to just — hold the line. We attack so we never have to find out what happens if we wait." He laughed, short and without any humor in it. "Scouts are circling. Concord. If I lose early, they pass me over, and then what was any of it for?"

Rin watched the boy beside them and understood, with a clarity that almost hurt, that Kael's cocky grin had never been arrogance at all. It was a sprint. A way of moving too fast to be caught standing in the moment where he might be found lacking. He had built a whole self out of motion so that no one — least of all his father — would ever see him stand still and be measured.

c7_rin_recognition.text:
Rin knew this shape. They knew it the way you know a song from its first three notes — not because they shared Kael's life, but because the wound underneath was the same wound, only worn outward instead of in.

Kael ran so no one could leave him standing alone. Rin had simply learned to be the one who left first.

Different strategies. The same fear at the bottom of both: that if anyone got a clear look at you, standing still, with nothing performed and nothing useful to offer, they would decide you were not worth keeping. Kael outran the verdict. Rin had spent a lifetime declining to be in the room when it was handed down.

It was easy, almost too easy, for Rin to see this in someone else. They had always been able to read a person's fear of being left — it was the one language they were fluent in, the way a sailor reads weather. What Rin had never once managed was to feel their own fear named back at them and not flinch away from it.

"You're not your wins," Rin said quietly. The words came out before the habit could stop them. "He's wrong about that. The thing that makes you worth having around isn't whether you cleaned up the match. Greywind doesn't run with you because you win. He runs with you because it's you."

Kael went still. For a moment Rin thought they had said too much, reached too far, and the old reflex rose up to take it back, to make a joke, to leave. But Kael only looked at them with a strange open hunger, the look of someone hearing a thing they had wanted said their whole life and had stopped believing they would ever hear.

c7_rin_opens.text:
"My turn, then," Kael said, recovering, nudging Rin's shoulder. "You know everything about everyone and nothing about yourself goes out the door. It's not fair. Tell me something true."

It was a small thing he was asking. Rin had given larger gifts to strangers and never blinked. But this — handing over one real piece of themselves to a person who might use it, who might leave with it, who might one day be gone and take it where Rin could never get it back — this made the wobble in their chest go tight and cold, the way the no-name core went flat every time they reached for the sign called Open and could not finish it.

The Coach had a word for what Rin was about to attempt, though he used it about blades. Open. The hardest sign. It did not command anything. It simply let the other thing in.

Rin looked at the dead-quiet blade in their palm and made themself do it.

"I grew up in a dish-hall like this one," they said. "Lower city. An orphan hall. The kind where the dishes are cracked and nobody fixes them because the kids spinning on them aren't worth the chalk." Their voice stayed level, which was its own small miracle. "I got adopted out twice. Sent back twice. After the second time I figured out it was safer not to want it. So I got small, and useful, and I never asked anybody to keep me. I learned to leave a place before it could decide it was done with me."

The hall was very quiet. Rin's heartbeat was loud in their own ears.

"This blade," they said, turning it, "was the first thing that didn't go anywhere. So I talk to it. That's the truth you wanted."

c7_kael_receives.text:
Rin braced for it without meaning to — the flicker of pity, the awkward shift, the careful change of subject that meant someone had heard more than they wanted to and was already calculating the distance back to safe ground. Rin had narrated a hundred such faces. They knew the early-warning signs by heart.

Kael's face did none of them.

He was quiet a moment, turning Rin's words over the way he turned his blade. Then he said, simply, "Two times. They sent you back two times." Not a question. He shook his head slowly, and what was in his face was not pity at all but something closer to anger, the clean protective kind, aimed at people he had never met. "Then they were idiots. Both of them. You hear me? Whoever sent you back didn't know what they had."

The wobble in Rin's chest did something it had never done before. It loosened.

"You don't have to leave first with me," Kael added, gruff now, embarrassed by his own sincerity and barreling through it the way he barreled through everything. "I'm a pain to get rid of. Ask anyone. I just attached myself to the best spinner in the lower bracket and I'm not going anywhere, so. You're stuck." He bumped his shoulder against Rin's again, harder. "Stuck," he repeated, like he was driving a stake into the ground.

Rin did not have words for what that did to them. They had given Kael one true thing, the smallest possible piece, fully expecting to feel the familiar drop of regret. Instead they felt, absurdly, lighter — as if the truth had weighed less once it was set down where someone could help carry it.

c7_blade_falters.text:
"Show me," Kael said suddenly, getting up, restless again but warmer with it. "You and that scrap of a blade. I want to see it spin when there's nobody to perform for."

The nearest practice dish sat in a pool of lamplight at the hall's center, its surface worn smooth by a thousand launches. Rin fitted the chipped blade to their old launcher, the ripcord stiff in the cold, and felt the familiar steadying that came whenever the blade was in their hands and the rest of the world narrowed to a single circle of stone.

Three. Two. One.

"Spirits, fly."

The blade leapt and bit into the dish and spun — and for a few bright seconds it was beautiful, the faint beast-shape stirring in the blur, that low warm hum answering up through Rin's wrist. Then something went wrong.

The note changed. Rin had spun this blade ten thousand times and knew its voice the way they knew their own pulse, and the voice it made now was thin and wrong, a high failing ring like a struck glass with a crack running through it. The warmth guttered. The faint shape in the blur flickered, went cold, went almost out — and the blade lurched off its line, wobbling hard, the chip in its rim catching and dragging at the stone.

It did not fall. But it nearly did. It scraped to a crooked, premature stop, listing, the core inside it gone dim and quiet in a way that frightened Rin more than any loss in the bracket had.

For one terrible breath the blade sat dead in the dish, and Rin felt the old, original fear rise up whole: that even this, even the one thing that had never left, was running out of whatever had kept it turning.

c7_the_worry.text:
Rin crouched and picked the blade up too fast, the way you reach for something falling. It was cold against their palm. Not the clean cold of metal at rest — a deeper cold, the cold of a held breath, of a core that had pushed past the edge of what its cracked body could give.

"It's old," Kael said carefully, crouching beside them. The teasing was gone. "How old?"

"I don't know. It was a hand-me-down when I got it, and that was six years ago." Rin turned it in the light. The chip in the rim had grown — they were almost sure of it — a hairline fracture spidering out from the original wound, the kind of damage that did not heal in a blade, only spread. "Scavenged. No-name. The kind nobody else wanted."

They did not say the rest, but it sat between them anyway. The later rounds would be harder. Mira read patterns no one else could see; the giant Brakk hit like a falling mountain; and beyond them, in the shadow of the bracket, the Masked Ace, who had never been beaten. Rin's whole climb depended on a blade that had just nearly died spinning a friendly practice match in an empty hall.

A scavenged blade against the strongest spinners alive. It had seemed like a story Rin could tell — the tailings kid and the no-name core. Now, holding the cold weight of it, the story felt like a thing that could break in their hands at the worst possible moment, and take everything they had only just begun to let themselves want down with it.

"Hey." Kael's voice. "It held. Look. It's still here."

It was. But it had never sounded like that before, and Rin could not un-hear it.

c7_pae_arrives.text:
"Is it broken?"

Pae stood at the edge of the lamplight in a too-big nightshirt, hair flattened on one side from a pillow, eyes wide and worried and fixed on the blade in Rin's hands. The younger orphan had a knack for materializing at exactly the wrong moment and exactly the right one, often both at once.

"You should be asleep," Rin said.

"I heard it sound funny." Pae crossed the floor on bare feet and dropped to a crouch beside them, peering at the chipped blade with the grave seriousness of someone half their height. "It made a sad sound. I know its happy sound and that wasn't it."

Something tightened in Rin's throat. The kid knew the blade's voices too. Of course they did — Pae had been watching Rin spin since they were small enough to need lifting onto the bench, idolizing the lower-city spinner who had never once told them to go away, even when Rin meant to, even when the habit of holding people at a half-step's distance whispered that they should.

"It's tired," Rin said, because it was the truest thing that wouldn't frighten the kid. "It worked hard today."

Pae nodded as if this were the most sensible thing in the world. Then they reached into the front of the nightshirt and produced, with enormous care, a length of cord — frayed, faded, clearly cut from some old launcher and saved for who knew how long in some private hiding place. They held it out in both hands like an offering.

"For luck," Pae said. "So it remembers it's not by itself."

c7_the_cord.text:
Rin looked at the frayed cord in the small outstretched hands and could not, for a moment, make their own hands move.

It was nothing. It was a scrap of worn ripcord a child had been hoarding, the kind of treasure that only counted as treasure to someone who owned almost nothing. By any reasonable measure it would do precisely nothing for a failing core. And yet Rin understood exactly what they were being handed, because they had once been a child who owned almost nothing too, and had poured the whole of their unwanted love into a single chipped blade because there was nowhere else for it to go.

Pae was doing now what Rin had done at nine. Giving everything to the thing they were most afraid of losing.

"Help me tie it," Rin said.

Pae's whole face opened with delight. Together they wound the frayed cord around the base of the launcher and knotted it, Pae's clumsy fingers and Rin's careful ones, until the faded scrap hung against the chipped metal like a small flag claimed for a country of two. Kael watched the whole thing with the soft, slightly stunned expression of a boy realizing he had wandered into something he hadn't known he was allowed to want either.

"There," Pae said, sitting back, fiercely satisfied. "Now it knows."

Rin turned the blade with its new cord in the lamplight. The core was still cold. The crack in the rim had not closed. Nothing about the blade's physical trouble was solved by a child's frayed ribbon.

But the wobble in Rin's chest had gone quiet — and that, Rin was slowly beginning to suspect, might be the entire point of everything.

c7_coach_watches.text:
From the deep shadow at the hall's far end, where four doors met and a single old man could stand unnoticed, the Coach watched the three of them around the dish.

He had come looking for Rin to talk strategy and had stopped at the threshold instead, held there by something he had not expected to feel and was not sure he could survive feeling for long. It was a small scene. A frayed cord, a tired blade, a swaggering boy gone gentle, a younger child fierce with a love too big for them. Nothing that would matter to anyone watching the bracket.

It mattered to him more than the bracket ever could.

Because Tovan — who had buried a name and a glory and a silenced beast in a hill-town twenty years ago, who had told himself he was done hoping, that hope was a thing that only ever cost you — stood in the dark and felt, in the deep cold place where a voice had gone quiet a generation back, the faintest stirring. Not a word. Not yet. Just the ghost of a turning, like a held breath beginning, almost, to let go.

He had trained Rin for reasons he had not yet told them, carrying a debt and a grief he kept hidden because hoping out loud terrified him more than any opponent ever had. He watched the orphan he had found spinning alone at dawn let two people in — actually in, past the counted exits and the careful distance — and he was glad, and he was afraid, and the gladness and the fear were the same thing.

They have no idea what's coming, he thought. The Masked Ace. The cold that took everything from me. And this blade is dying.

He stepped back into the dark before they could see his face, and let them have the lamplight a while longer.

c8_watched.text:
Rin had spun in front of crowds for three rounds now, and they had learned the particular weight of being looked at. The Gauntlet crowd had looked at them like a curiosity. Kael had looked at them like an obstacle, and then, after, like a friend. But the girl waiting across the practice dish looked at Rin the way Rin looked at a room they had just entered—counting, measuring, filing away the exits.

It was not a comfortable thing to be on the other side of.

She sat very straight on the bench, a slim figure in the grey-and-silver of a Concord club, her dark hair pinned back so severely that not a strand moved when she turned her head. A fox-blade rested in her open palm, lacquered the deep red of a banked fire, nine fine etched lines fanning from its crown like tails. She was not warming up. She was not stretching the cord of her launcher the way every other competitor in the hall did, fidgeting off their nerves. She was simply watching Rin, and had been, Rin realized, for some time.

Kael nudged Rin's shoulder, lowering his voice in a way that for Kael was nearly a whisper. "That's Mira," he said. "Don't let the quiet fool you. They say she's never lost a match she'd already watched the other spinner play. And she watches everyone." He paused, and something uncharacteristically uneasy crossed his face. "She's watched you, Rin. All of you. Every Gauntlet round. Sat right there and didn't blink."

Rin met the girl's gaze across the chalk-dusted floor. There was no challenge in it, no smugness, none of the heat Kael wore. Only attention—total, patient, unhurried attention—and behind that, a stillness Rin could not read at all. It was, Rin thought, like being looked at by a closed door.
c8_watched.title: The Strategist's Eye

c8_solved_on_paper.text:
Mira rose and crossed the floor without hurry, and when she stopped before Rin she did not offer her hand. She studied them a moment longer—the chipped blade in Rin's grip, the frayed launcher cord Pae had tied around it for luck, the way Rin's weight had already shifted, without their meaning it, toward the nearest door.

"You count exits," Mira said. It was not a question. Her voice was clean and even, every word set down exactly where she wanted it. "In the Gauntlet, third round, the cadet feinted left and you didn't follow. Everyone followed. You didn't, because you'd already decided he was lying with his whole body and telling the truth with his blade. That was the moment I knew you were worth watching."

Rin said nothing. Their pulse had picked up—that small wobble in the chest, the old animal warning that they had been seen too clearly, too fast.

"I've studied every match you've ever spun," Mira went on, and there was no boast in it; she might have been reciting weather. "I know which way you break under pressure. I know that you win by reading your opponent better than they read themselves, which is a thing I also do, so I know exactly what it costs and exactly where it fails." A small, precise pause. "I know you, Rin of the lower city. I've solved you on paper."

It should have sounded like a threat. Strangely, it didn't. It sounded almost lonely, the way a person sounds when they have spent so long being the smartest one in every room that being right has stopped feeling like anything at all.

c8_fox_lore.text:
She turned the fox-blade so Rin could see it fully, and for the first time something in the flat surface of her shifted—not warmth, exactly, but a crack of it, quickly closed.

"Sumi," she said. "My partner."

In the lacquered red, Rin caught the faint blur of a beast-shape, the way you catch a face in firelight: a fox, lean and watchful, nine tails coiled close as if braced for a blow that had not yet come and was assumed to be coming. Rin had learned by now that a blade was a mirror, that a beast carried whatever its spinner carried. Kael's wolf over-attacked because Kael fought to outrun the quiet. And Sumi—Sumi watched the exits too.

"She's been read her whole life," Mira said, and now her voice had gone very careful, as if she were translating something out of a language she did not like to speak. "Concord trains the nine-tailed lines to be perfect instruments. You learn what your handler wants. You learn to be useful before you're wanted, because useful is the thing that keeps you. Sumi is the finest reading-fox in the guild." She looked down at the blade. "I have never once asked her what she wants. I'm not certain the question would mean anything to her. We were not made for it."

Rin felt something turn over in their chest, low and uncomfortable, because they knew that shape. Useful before you're wanted. They had built a whole life on it. Across the dish stood a girl who had built the same life from the other end—who had decided that if she could simply know everyone, she would never need to be known by anyone, and would therefore never be left. Two people, Rin thought, wearing the same armor backwards.

c8_modern_weaving.text:
"You spin the old way," Mira said. "The bonded way. The Wardens love you for it." She said Wardens the way one might name a beautiful, obsolete machine. "Concord trained me on modern weaving. Efficient signs. Clean lines. We're taught that feeling is noise—static between you and the read. A spinner who feels is a spinner who flinches, and a spinner who flinches loses to one who doesn't." She recited it smoothly, a lesson worn down by a thousand repetitions. "It's correct. The numbers are not arguable. We win."

"Then why are you telling me this," Rin said. It was the first thing they'd said, and it came out quieter than they intended.

For a heartbeat Mira didn't answer. Something moved behind her eyes, the way deep water moves under ice—there and gone, a thing she had not authorized.

"Because the numbers have started to bother me," she said at last, very low, as though admitting it to the blade and not to Rin. "I can predict every spinner in this bracket. All of them. I run the patterns and the patterns hold." Her jaw tightened, the only crack in all that composure. "And there is one spinner I cannot run. The masked one. Raze. I have watched his matches frame by frame and the cold goes off him in waves and his beast—" She stopped herself. Filed it away. The door closed again. "It doesn't matter. That's not our match. Ours is next."

But Rin had heard it. The unease under the certainty. The smartest girl in the room had finally found a thing she couldn't solve, and instead of fear, what crossed her face for that half-second had looked, impossibly, like relief.

c8_the_unmodelable.text:
Rin had spent fifteen years learning to read the moment a person was about to leave—the half-turn of a shoulder, the apology already forming in the eyes. It had kept them safe and it had kept them alone, and it had made them, without their ever wanting the skill, very good at understanding people who hid.

So they understood Mira.

She was afraid. Not of losing—losing was a number, and she had made her peace with numbers. She was afraid of what she would be if she were ever not the one who knew. If she stopped being the smartest mind in the hall, what was left? She had filed away her whole heart as noise to be filtered, the same way Sumi had been filed away as an instrument, and somewhere in all that precision she had quietly stopped being a person to anyone, including herself. Rin recognized it the way you recognize your own handwriting on a wall.

And in recognizing it, Rin saw the one thing Mira could not predict.

She could model a feint. She could model fear, fatigue, the exact angle at which Rin's blade would fail under load. She had run every pattern Rin had ever made. But a pattern was a thing you did to win. Mira had never had to account for a spinner who, in the deciding instant, might choose to do something for a reason that had nothing to do with winning at all—who might care more about the person across the dish than the crown above it. There was no column in her ledger for that. It was the one variable she had spent her life filtering out, and so it was the one she would never see coming.

The knowing of it settled in Rin's chest, steady and strange. Not a weapon. A door.

c8_approach_choice.text:
"They're calling our dish," Mira said. The arena beyond the practice hall had begun its low, expectant roar. She tucked a strand of hair that had not moved back into place anyway, a tell Rin filed without meaning to. "However you mean to spin this, spin it. I've already seen all of it."

She believed that. Rin could change it.

choices.label: Praise her skill honestly, and spin a clean, fair match.
Push the pace—overwhelm her before she can ever plan.

c8_kind_branch.text:
Rin let the moment breathe. They thought of all the things they could say to rattle her, and set every one of them down.

"You're the best reader I've ever stood across from," Rin said. Plainly. No edge. "You saw the feint in the third round. Nobody saw that. I barely saw it, and I made it." They watched Mira's careful face, watched her brace for the trick that surely followed honest praise, the way a person braces who has only ever been complimented as a setup. "There's no trap in that. It's just true. You're going to make me spin better than I know how, and I want a clean match. A fair one. Whatever happens after, I want us both to have meant it."

Mira went still. Properly still—not her watching-stillness, but the stillness of a person who has just been handed something they did not request and do not know where to put down. She had walked into the hall armored against being studied, against being beaten, against being mocked. She had no defense at all against being respected.

"That's—" she started, and the clean machinery of her voice caught for the first time. "That's not a useful thing to say before a match. It doesn't gain you anything."

"No," Rin agreed. "It doesn't."

Something complicated moved across Mira's face—suspicion, then confusion, then, very briefly, before she pinned it down and filed it away with all the rest, a kind of ache. She gripped the fox-blade a little closer. In its red lacquer, Rin could have sworn the watchful little beast-shape tilted its head, as if it had heard, faintly, a question it had waited its whole life to be asked.

c8_fierce_branch.text:
Rin let the calm leave their shoulders and the fire come up instead. If Mira had solved them on paper, then Rin would spin a match that lived faster than paper could be written.

"You've watched every match I've ever played," Rin said, and there was heat in it now, a banked grin under the words. "Good. Then you already know I don't fight the spinner you studied. I fight the one standing in front of me, right now, and I'm not going to give you a single quiet second to run your numbers." They rolled the chipped blade once across their knuckles, the frayed cord whispering. "You like time. You like to read, and plan, and know. So I'm going to take the time away. From the first count I'm coming at you, and I'm not going to stop, and you're going to have to feel your way through this one instead of thinking it."

Mira's chin lifted a fraction. It was not fear—Rin saw that clearly. It was something nearer to hunger. She had spent her whole life knowing the answer before the question finished, and here was someone promising to move faster than her certainty could keep up.

"You think speed beats a read," she said. The clean voice had an edge to it now, a brightness. "It doesn't. I'll have you mapped inside three exchanges."

"Then map fast," Rin said.

The corner of Mira's mouth did something it clearly had not been trained to do. In the red lacquer of the fox-blade, the lean little beast-shape seemed to crouch lower, tails gathering—not in fear, Rin thought, but the way a thing braces when, for once, it does not already know how the chase will end.

c8_ready_signs.text:
They walked to the dish together, the great arena rising around them in tiers of held breath. Rin had stopped being surprised by the size of it—the way the roar of the crowd could press on the chest like a hand—but the silence that came after, the moment the spinners stepped to their marks, still raised the hair on their arms. Forty thousand people leaned in, and the world narrowed to a circle of polished stone and the person standing on the other side of it.

The Coach was somewhere in the competitors' tier, Rin knew, his face doing the still, careful thing it did. Kael had found a seat at the rail and was almost certainly already too loud. And Pae—Pae would be perched wherever they could see, eyes huge, watching Rin the way Rin had once watched the chipped blade: like proof that someone could stay.

Mira set her feet. She raised her hands and began the readying weave, and even her signs were beautiful—spare, exact, not a gesture wasted, the modern style honed to a blade's edge. Listen. Steady. Each one landed perfectly. There was not a flaw in it anywhere, and that, Rin thought, was the whole of her: flawless, and braced, and alone inside the flawlessness.

Rin lifted their own hands. Their signs were rougher, the old bonded way, asking rather than commanding. They reached the readying breath and felt the chipped blade answer—faint, faithful, the way it always answered, a small warm pressure against the cold of the open arena. Steady, Rin told it, and themself. We've done harder than smart.

Across the dish, Mira's eyes found Rin's and held. Whatever Rin had chosen in the hall, she had felt it land. She had not been able to file it away.

c8_launch_cliff.text:
The referee stepped to the rim of the dish, arm raised. The arena drew one long breath and held it.

Rin set the chipped blade to the launcher and drew the cord taut. The frayed luck-string Pae had tied bit gently into their palm. Through it, faintly, the no-name beast pressed back—closer tonight than it had been in the Gauntlet, Rin thought, though still it gave no name, still it kept that one last door shut. Soon, Rin promised it, without knowing what they were promising. Soon.

Mira's fox-blade hummed at her own launcher, low and red, the nine etched tails catching the arena light. She was not smiling. She was not frowning. She had gone entirely into the place where she did her reading, that cold clear room behind her eyes—but for the first time, Rin understood, she had walked into a match unable to see the end of it. The girl who always knew did not know. And under the dread of that, Rin had seen it: relief, like a window cracked in a sealed room.

The referee's voice rang out over the hush, the count that every spinner in the Spun World learned before they learned their own name.

"Three—"

Rin's grip settled. Steady.

"Two—"

Mira's eyes narrowed to a reader's focus.

"One—"

And the whole stadium exhaled into one cry, forty thousand voices and two spinners and the oldest words in the sport, as the cords released and the blades fell screaming toward the dish:

"Spirits, fly!"

c9_open_arena.text:
The arena had gone the particular kind of quiet that only a full crowd can make — thousands of held breaths stacked into one. Rin stood at the lip of the dish and felt the cold polish of it under their soles, the ring of chalk dust someone had swept into a perfect circle, the faint warmth still rising off the metal where the last match had burned. Across from them, Mira waited the way a clock waits: without impatience, without doubt, every part of her already in motion toward an outcome she had decided on hours ago.

She had watched every match Rin had ever spun. She had said so without a trace of cruelty, the way another spinner might mention the weather. And Rin believed her, because that was the unsettling thing about Mira — she did not bluff. She simply knew, and let you stand inside the knowing until it made you smaller.

Rin set the chipped blade against their launcher. The frayed cord Pae had tied around the base for luck pressed a thin braid into their palm. They counted the exits without deciding to: two tunnels, the judges' gallery, the long stairs to the stands. The old habit, the one that had kept them safe their whole life. Then they made themselves stop.

Because somewhere up in the noise were Kael's stupid grin and the Coach's still, watchful face, and that changed the math of the room in a way Rin did not have a word for yet. They only knew the wobble in their chest had not quite gone quiet, and that for once they did not entirely want it to.

The referee raised a hand. The crowd inhaled.
c9_open_arena.title: Mind Against Mind

choices.label: Unleash your spirit-beast
Read her pattern, then counter
Defend, and outlast her

c9_br_unleash.text:
Rin stopped trying to be smarter than the smartest person in the room. They could not out-calculate Mira; no one could. So they did the thing the math could not hold — they let go.

'Listen,' they breathed, and then, faster than the sign was meant to be woven, 'Turn — Release.' The chipped blade screamed up out of Sumi's careful cage, not along any line Mira had drawn but through the wall of it, a wild diagonal that crossed every prediction at once. For an instant the beast in the blur showed itself — a shape with no name, leaning into the spin like a runner finally let off the leash.

Mira's eyes widened a fraction. It was the smallest tell in the world, and on her it was an earthquake.

Sumi pivoted to compensate, nine tails snapping into a new formation, but the fox had been built to answer a plan, and there was no plan now — only Rin and the blade and the raw forward want of a beast that had spent its whole life being told to be careful. The two blades met at the center with a sound like a struck bell. Sumi's perfect arcs scattered.

The no-name core was singing — not louder, but truer, the way a voice does when it stops pretending. Rin felt it answer in their chest before it answered in the dish, that flicker of warmth that had nothing to do with winning and everything to do with finally being heard. They were not spinning to beat Mira. They were spinning the way they spun alone at dawn, when no one was watching and there was nothing to protect.

Mira saw that, too. And something in her composed face began, very slightly, to come apart.

c9_br_counter.text:
Mira had a pattern for everything Rin could do — every angle, every feint, every conservative bleed of momentum Rin might spend to survive. She had filed Rin under a category and closed the drawer. So Rin gave her the one move that had no category.

They waited. They let Sumi's nine tails herd the chipped blade exactly where Mira wanted it, into the kill-pocket at the dish's low edge, and they did not fight it. Mira's brow tightened — this was too easy, and she knew too easy was a trap, but she could not find the trap because there wasn't one yet.

Then, instead of countering Sumi, Rin countered Mira. 'Open,' they whispered — the sign they had failed a thousand times, the one that could not be faked. And for half a heartbeat, instead of reaching for advantage, Rin reached for the girl across the dish: I see you. I see how alone it is, being the only one who ever knows the answer.

The blade turned on that feeling. Not a calculated line — a chosen one. It slipped Sumi's pocket from the inside, the way water leaves a cupped hand, and struck the fox-blade square where Mira had left it undefended because no spinner fighting to win would ever have made that move.

Sumi rang and wobbled. Mira's lips parted. She had modeled the variable Rin spun with as noise to be filtered — and it had just walked straight through the center of her perfect equation and rearranged it.

'That's not—' she started, and stopped, because there was no word in her vocabulary for what Rin had just done. Caring more about the opponent than the win. The one thing she could not predict, because she had never once tried it herself.

c9_br_defend.text:
Mira's plan was a knife, and a knife needs something to cut. So Rin gave her nothing.

They drew the chipped blade in tight, close to the dish's heart, and wove 'Steady — Hold,' the patient signs, the ones the Coach said most spinners skipped because they were boring. Sumi came at them in wave after elegant wave, nine tails fanning every approach Mira had drawn in her head, and every time Rin simply absorbed it — slid sideways, bled the angle, let the fox spend itself against a thing that would not break.

Mira's strategy assumed Rin would push back. It had no answer for a spinner content to endure. Each exchange that should have ended it merely passed, and Rin's blade kept turning, low and certain, the frayed luck-cord blurred to a thin gold ring.

This was the thing Rin had always been good at, long before any of this. Outlasting. Staying when staying cost something. They had survived a whole childhood by becoming the thing that did not break and did not ask, and for once that wound was a weapon, and it was beautiful.

Sumi's spin began to thin. Mira had spent her certainty in the first thirty seconds, the way she always did, and there was nothing held in reserve because Mira kept nothing in reserve — not in a dish, not anywhere. When the fox-blade finally faltered, Rin's chipped core was still humming, unhurried, alive.

Across the dish, Mira stared at a blade that had simply refused to be solved. For the first time in her competitive life, the smartest person in the room had run out of room — and she did not look angry about it. She looked, of all things, relieved.

c9_rejoin_win.text:
Sumi's spin gave out with a sound like a long breath releasing. The nine tails folded; the fox-blade settled, wobbled, and lay still in the chalk. For a moment no one in the entire arena moved, as if the crowd were waiting for Mira to produce the counter she always had, the read no one else had seen.

She did not produce it. She looked down at her quieted blade, and then up at Rin, and her face — that smooth, impenetrable face that gave away nothing because giving things away was inefficient — simply opened.

Rin's first instinct, the old one, was to soften the win, to apologize, to make themself small so the loss would hurt the other person less. They had done it a hundred times. They opened their mouth to do it now.

But Mira spoke first.

'I knew everything you were going to do,' she said, quiet enough that it was only for the dish, not the stands. 'Every angle. I had you mapped before the count.' She shook her head once, slowly, as though dislodging something. 'And then you did a thing I had no line for. You weren't spinning to win. You were spinning to — '

She stopped. The word she needed was not a strategy word, and those were the only words she had ever been taught to trust.

The referee's hand came down. The win was Rin's, formally, officially, the bracket already redrawing itself in the great board above the gate. But Rin barely heard the announcement. They were watching the most reserved person they had ever met stand in the middle of a defeat and look, impossibly, grateful for it.

c9_mira_offer.text:
Mira crossed the dish to retrieve her blade, and Rin braced for the cool, clinical handshake of a professional who had simply lost an event. Instead Mira crouched, lifted Sumi from the chalk with a tenderness Rin had not expected, and turned the dull fox-blade over in her fingers as if seeing it for the first time.

'They used her for her reads,' Mira said. She did not look up. 'My handlers. From the time I was six. Sumi sees patterns no other beast can see, so they pointed her at opponents like an instrument and measured what came back. No one ever asked her what she wanted. No one asked me, either.' A short, dry laugh, aimed at herself. 'I assumed that was just what a bond was. A very precise tool you learn to operate.'

Then she stood, and she did the thing that undid Rin completely. She held out her hand — not the brusque grip of a sealed match, but an offer, palm open.

'Teach me,' Mira said. 'Not the signs. I can copy the signs in an afternoon. Teach me the thing you did. How you let her in.' Her voice stayed level, but her eyes did not. 'I have spent my whole life being the one who reads the room. I would like, one day, to be — known. The way you just knew me.'

The girl who could predict anyone was asking to be surprised by being seen. Rin looked at the open hand and felt the floor of their certainty shift, because somewhere in the last sixty seconds they had stopped being able to hold Mira at arm's length, and they had not even noticed it happen.

They took her hand.

c9_kael_arrives.text:
Kael came down the stands two at a time, vaulting the last rail with the grace of someone who knew exactly how good he looked doing it, and arrived at the dish-side already mid-sentence.

'Did you see that? Did everyone see that? She had you boxed — I have seen Mira box people, it is genuinely upsetting to watch — and you just—' He made a gesture that was supposed to represent the entire match and mostly looked like he was swatting a bee. 'I don't even know what you did. Mira, what did they do?'

'I don't know either,' Mira said, and there was a new, unguarded note in it. 'That's rather the point.'

Kael blinked at the two of them — at the easy way Mira was standing beside Rin now, at the handshake that had clearly meant something — and Rin watched him do a quick recalculation, the same one Rin was doing. Yesterday there had been one person who chose Rin and stayed. Now there were two.

'Right,' Kael declared, throwing an arm around Mira's shoulders with the confidence of a man who had decided they were all friends and would brook no appeal. Mira went very still, the way a cat does when picked up against its will, but she did not move away. 'Then we're a unit now. Rin's corner. I called it first, for the record. Mira's second.'

'I am not anyone's second,' Mira said.

'Co-first,' Kael allowed.

And Rin, standing between them in the slowly emptying arena, felt the wobble in their chest do something it had never done before — it did not warn them of an exit. It just, for a moment, settled, like a blade finding its center.

c9_rin_alarm.text:
They should have been only glad. That was the maddening part.

Rin had won. They had climbed another rung of a bracket that had no business letting a tailings kid this far, and two of the most gifted spinners in the tournament were standing at their shoulder calling themselves Rin's corner. By every measure Rin had ever used to keep score of a life, this was the best day they had ever had.

And underneath the gladness, very quietly, was the old cold thing — the one that had kept them alive.

Because it was easy, before. Friendship at arm's length was free; it cost nothing to lose what you had never let close. Rin had spent fifteen years perfecting the art of the half-step back, the warmth that never quite became need, so that when people left — and people always left, that was the one law Rin trusted completely — there would be nothing in the chest to tear.

But Mira's open hand was not at arm's length. Kael's stupid arm around Mira's shoulders was not at arm's length. And Rin understood, with a lurch like missing a stair, that they had started to need these people. Not their skill. Not their company in a tournament that would end. Them.

Which meant that somewhere out past the crown and the prize money, there was now a version of the future that could actually hurt — a day when the tournament closed and everyone scattered back to their own lives and Rin was, once more, the one left standing in an empty dish-hall.

The thought arrived fully formed and terrible: I have given them something to take back.

Rin smiled at Kael's joke, because it was funny, and counted no exits, and was quietly, privately, afraid.

c9_to_replays.text:
They found a viewing alcove off the competitors' hall — a narrow room with a scrying-glass the officials used to review disputed matches, the dish-light still humming in it from someone else's replay. Mira had asked to stay, ostensibly to study the next bracket. Rin suspected it was something gentler than that: she had nowhere in particular she belonged to be, and now there was a corner that was hers.

Kael sprawled across two chairs and narrated the tournament standings with the authority of a man who had memorized them precisely to seem casual about them. Pae had appeared from somewhere — Pae always appeared from somewhere — and was perched on the arm of Rin's chair, vibrating with secondhand triumph, retelling Rin's own match back to Rin with embellishments that grew with each pass.

'And then the fox did the nine-tail thing,' Pae said, eyes enormous, 'and I thought, that's it, that's the end, and then you just—'

'I was there,' Rin said gently.

'I know! It was amazing!'

Mira was not listening. She had pulled the scrying-glass toward herself and was scrolling back through the official archive — not Rin's matches, Rin noticed, but the other side of the bracket. The undefeated side. The footage flickered, found a figure, and held: a masked spinner in a practice dish, alone, his blade carving the air with a precision so total it had no joy in it at all.

Raze.

Mira leaned in. The easy warmth went out of her face and the old, terrible focus came back — but pointed, this time, at something that frightened even her.

c9_mira_sees.text:
'Watch his fourth sign,' Mira said.

The room had gone quiet without anyone deciding to. Even Pae had stopped talking. On the scrying-glass, the masked figure wove a familiar sequence — Listen, Steady, Turn — and then a fourth shape Rin's eyes slid off of, the way you slide off a word spelled wrong, knowing it's wrong before you can say how.

'That should be Open,' Mira said. 'It isn't. He's bending the sign backward. Look at the wrist — it's a hair too sharp, too closed. He isn't asking the beast in. He's—' she searched for it, and landed on a word that made the back of Rin's neck go cold ' — ordering it. Compelling. Every spinner I was trained with does it a little, for efficiency. He's doing it completely.'

Rin remembered, suddenly and bodily, the practice-yard at the gate days ago — the cold under-feeling that had come off Raze's blade and crawled up Rin's spine before they had a name for it. They had felt this without understanding it. Mira was simply giving it words.

'There's more.' Mira tracked back, froze a frame, pointed. In the blur of Raze's blade, for a single instant, the ghost of a beast showed — and flinched. Not from the opponent. From its own spinner. 'See that? His beast is pulling away from him. Every clean win he stacks up, it pulls further.' She sat back, and her clinical voice had a hairline crack running through it now. 'He's winning by going deaf to the thing that powers him. The cold signs work. That's the horror of it. They just keep working, right up until there's nothing left on the other end of the line to answer.'

Kael had stopped sprawling. 'Going deaf,' he repeated quietly. 'You're saying the Masked Ace is — what, losing his beast? On purpose?'

'On doctrine,' Mira said. 'Which is worse.'

c9_mira_cold_lore.text:
Rin thought of the Coach going still at the gate, the way his whole face had closed like a shutter at the sight of that joyless, perfect style. He had refused to explain it then. Now Rin understood that he had recognized it — that whatever this cold thing was, it was old, and it had a history, and the Coach was somewhere in that history in a place he would not talk about.

'The Coach showed me a sign like that once,' Rin said slowly. 'A cold one. Just once, to forbid it. It worked instantly — it was the easiest thing I'd ever felt on a launcher — and the blade's beast flinched away from him. He wouldn't say how he knew it.' Rin looked at the masked figure frozen mid-spin in the glass, that terrible solitude wrapped in mastery. 'I think it scares him. More than anyone we've fought scares him.'

Mira nodded, slow. 'It should scare all of us. Because if the most dominant spinner of our generation is winning the whole tournament with a style that quietly murders his own bond, then when he takes the crown, that becomes the lesson. That becomes what every dish-hall teaches the next ten years of kids. Win cold. Need nothing.' She said it flatly, but Rin heard the personal weight under it — Mira had been raised on the gentler end of exactly that creed, taught that feeling was noise, and she was only now, in this small humming room full of people who had chosen her, beginning to suspect what it had cost her.

Pae's voice came small from the arm of the chair. 'Can't the judges stop him? If he's, you know. Cheating his own beast?'

The three older spinners exchanged a look. It was Mira who answered, and it was not the answer Pae wanted.

'That,' she said, 'is the part I'm afraid of.'

c9_mira_money.text:
Mira pushed the replay aside and pulled up something else — not match footage now but columns, the dense administrative bones of the tournament that no spectator ever saw. Sponsorship ledgers. Council rosters. The dry machinery beneath the glory.

'I read these for fun,' she admitted, when Kael made a face. 'Patterns are patterns. People hide them in numbers because they think no one reads the numbers.' Her finger traced a line down a roster of names — the judging council, the panel of Bond-Wardens and appointed officials who would rule on the final. 'These are the judges for the grand final. Old law says only true bonds compete, and the Wardens are supposed to see whether a beast answers freely. But look who funds them now.'

She overlaid a second column. The same patron crest appeared again and again beside the council names, frost-pale, elegant, everywhere. Concord.

'They've bought the council,' Mira said quietly. 'Not all of it. But enough. Enough that if the Masked Ace's beast is going silent right there on the dish in front of them — if his bond is a forced, half-deaf thing that should disqualify him under the oldest rule there is — these judges will look at it and call it clean.' She let the columns hang in the air between them. 'There's exactly one name on this roster their money hasn't reached. One Warden old enough to still see a true bond and stubborn enough to say so. Oru. And she's outvoted before she opens her mouth.'

The humming little room was very still. Outside, faintly, the crowd was roaring for some other match, some other dream still intact. In here, four people sat with the shape of the thing they were actually up against, and it was bigger than any blade.

'So the final's already decided,' Kael said. It wasn't quite a question.

'The final,' Mira said, 'is rigged.'

c9_resolve_together.text:
The word sat in the room like a dropped weight. Rigged. It meant that all of this — the climb, the chipped blade, the impossible run of a tailings kid through a bracket that ate prodigies — might be a story with its ending already written by people Rin would never meet, in a language of ledgers and patronage Rin had never been taught to read.

The old instinct rose up clean and familiar: walk away. Take the rounds already won, take the small dignity of having gotten further than anyone expected, and leave before the rigged door closed on them. It would not even hurt much. It never did, when you left first.

Rin looked around the little room instead.

Pae, watching Rin's face for permission to be afraid. Kael, jaw set, a boy who had finally found something worth being brave about that wasn't his father's approval. And Mira — Mira who had been raised to need no one and had spent the last hour quietly choosing the opposite — waiting, palm-open in a way that had nothing to do with the match anymore, to see whether Rin would let her help carry this.

'We tell the Coach,' Rin heard themself say. 'All of it. The cold signs, the council, Oru.' Their voice did not shake, which surprised them. 'And then we don't run.'

Kael grinned like a struck match. Mira nodded once, the deal sealed cleaner than any handshake. Pae sat up straighter, lifted by it.

And Rin stood in the center of the first room in their life they had not bothered to count the exits of, terrified in an entirely new direction — not of being left, for once, but of how much it would cost to stay — and found that the wobble in their chest, for the length of one breath, had steadied into something that turned alongside them and did not let them spin alone.

The no-name blade, in their hand, was warm.

c10_after_mira.text:
The practice hall the stewards gave them between rounds was an afterthought of a room, tucked under the Coliseum's east stair where the crowd-roar arrived as a muffled tide that rose and fell without ever quite ending.
