A single dish stood at its center, older than the arena above it, its rim worn smooth by a hundred years of hands. Dust hung in the lamplight. The air smelled of cold stone and the faint, oily ghost of hot metal, and Rin breathed it in like the only thing in Coilspire that did not want something from them.

Mira's loss was three hours old. Kael had gone to find food and not come back, which meant he had found people to talk at instead. Mira herself was somewhere with her replays, hunting the thing she had glimpsed in the Masked Ace's spinning and could not yet name. So it was only the two of them now — Rin and the Coach — the way it had been at the start, before there was a bracket or a crown or a table Rin was beginning, dangerously, to want a seat at.

The Coach sat on the low bench against the wall. He was turning something over in his hands, slow, the way a person worries a stone. Rin had seen him do it a hundred times and never once looked closely, because looking closely was a thing Rin did not do to people they intended to keep. Now, with the hall quiet and the win still ringing thin in their chest, they looked.

It was a blade. Old. Dull as a swallowed coin. And though the Coach's hands moved over it with terrible care, it did not so much as breathe.
c10_after_mira.title: The Spirit-Sage

c10_the_dull_blade.text:
Rin had assumed, the way you assume the shape of a thing seen only at the edge of sight, that the Coach did not spin. Plenty of trainers didn't. The great ones taught from the rim of the dish, hands behind their backs, letting the student make every mistake there was. It had never occurred to Rin that a man could teach the Six Signs with such bone-deep certainty and yet never once launch a blade of his own.

The thing in his hands answered the question and asked a worse one.

It had been beautiful, once. Rin could see that under the dullness, the way you can see the shape of a face in an old photograph gone to fog. An elk reared along its crown, antlers swept back into the curve of the rim, the lines of it proud and certain and made by someone who had loved the making. But the spirit-blur a living blade wore even at rest — that faint, breathing shimmer Rin had felt off every core they'd ever held, even the cold ones — was simply not there. The blade sat in the Coach's palm like a stone in a riverbed. Heavy. Quiet. Done.

"You're staring," the Coach said, not unkindly.

"I've never seen you hold a blade." Rin's voice came out smaller than they meant it to. "Not once."

"No." He did not look up from it. His thumb moved along the elk's antler, found a notch worn there by years of the same gesture, and stopped. "I haven't launched a blade in twenty years." A breath. "This one won't launch. It hasn't turned since the night it went quiet." He finally raised his eyes to Rin, and there was something in them Rin had no name for yet. "Sit down. I should have told you this a long while ago."

c10_the_confession.text:
Rin sat. Across the small room their knees nearly touched, and Rin felt the old reflex fire — the count of exits, the door at their back, the window high in the far wall — and made themself ignore it. The Coach was not a threat. The Coach was the closest thing Rin had ever had to a fixed point, and a fixed point was its own kind of danger, because if it moved, everything moved.

"You know the Tournament has a history," he said. "Every kid in every dish-hall knows the names. The champions. The ones who got crowned and the ones who should have." He turned the dull blade once more. "There was a man, a generation ago. They called him the Spirit-Sage. The last true Bond-Sage. He could wake a core no one else could reach and weave the open-hand at will, and for nine years no one in the world could beat him, because he didn't fight the blade across the dish — he reached past it, to the spinner, and made even his enemies feel briefly less alone." He smiled, but it was a terrible smile, the kind that costs something. "People wrote songs. You've probably sung one without knowing whose it was."

Rin had. Suddenly they were sure of it. A dish-hall round the younger orphans chanted while they spun, a name in it worn so smooth by repetition that no one remembered it had ever belonged to a real person.

"Coach," Rin said.

"Tovan." He said his own name like a thing dug up. "My name is Tovan. And the elk on this blade is — was — mine. I was the Spirit-Sage. And I am the only champion in the history of the Bond Tournament to walk out of this Coliseum and let the world believe he had died."

c10_the_silence_lore.text:
The crowd-tide rose somewhere above them and fell. Rin did not move. There is a kind of news that rearranges the room it is spoken in, and Rin sat very still inside the rearrangement, waiting for the floor to settle.

"You've heard the word," Tovan said. "The Silence. The thing the old spinners cross their fingers against. You know it the way you know a story is frightening without knowing why."

"It's when a beast goes quiet," Rin said carefully. "For good."

"It's worse than that." He set the blade flat on his knee, as if it needed both his hands free to be said. "A beast is a fragment of the First Spin — a living will, nested in a thing that turns. You can wound a bond. You can frighten a beast, drive it deep, make it wary. All of that heals, given a true hand and time. But there is a cruelty in the cold signs — a way of spinning a blade out that doesn't merely beat the beast, it betrays it so completely that the beast retreats past hearing. Not dead. That's the horror of it. Trapped. Awake somewhere too deep to reach, in a blade that will never spin true again." His jaw worked. "No one has ever woken a silenced beast. Not in all the centuries of this sport. It is the one thing we say cannot be undone. It is why the cold signs are the great taboo — not because they lose, but because of what they're capable of doing to the very thing they claim to master."

Rin looked at the dull elk on his knee and understood, with a lurch that had nowhere to land, that they had been carrying a tomb from town to town without knowing it. "Your elk," they said. "It's not asleep."

"No," Tovan said. "It is silent. Twenty years silent. And I am the man who got it that way."

c10_vehesal_named.text:
He told it plainly, which was worse than if he had wept. Plainness, Rin was learning, was how Tovan carried the heaviest things.

"I had a friend," he said. "Not a rival the way the songs like to pretend. A friend. We came up together in halls poorer than yours, two boys with two blades and no one watching, and we made each other better than either of us could have managed alone. His name was Vehesal."

The name meant nothing to Rin and everything to the room. Tovan let it sit there a moment, the way you set down something you have carried a long way.

"He was my equal. My better, some days. And then one year he lost a match he was certain — certain — he deserved to win, and something in him decided the loss was a lie the world had told him. He decided that caring was just a handle other people grab to break you by. So he set out to prove it." Tovan's hands had gone still. "He severed his own bond. On purpose. Cut himself loose from his own beast so it could never be used against him, and in the hollow where the bond had been he built the cold signs — signs that compel instead of ask. They work. That's the obscenity of it. They work beautifully. A cold spinner can beat almost anyone in the world while going slowly, quietly deaf to the spirit that powers them, and never feel the loss, because they have decided the loss is strength."

He looked at Rin. "In our last duel he spun my blade out with a cold sign crueler than anything I'd believed a person could weave. My elk fell silent on this dish, in front of the world. And it has never woken since."

c10_the_real_guilt.text:
Rin waited for the rest, because they had spent their whole life reading the spaces in what people said, and there was a space here, jagged at the edges.

"You blame yourself," Rin said. "But not for losing."

Tovan looked at them for a long moment, and something in his weathered face came undone — not collapse, just a loosening, as if a knot held so long it had become part of the rope was finally, carefully, being worked free.

"No. Not for losing." His voice dropped. "For how I spun that night. I knew Vehesal. I knew the wound under the cold — I'd watched it open. And when we faced each other on this dish for the last time, I had a choice. I could have reached for him. Wove the open-hand and let him feel, just once more, that he was not the thing he'd convinced himself he was. That he was still known. Still — " he stopped, started again. "Instead I wanted to win. I wanted to beat him so badly the whole world would see I was right and he was wrong, and I poured everything into the beating and nothing into the reaching. And while I was busy proving my point, my friend went somewhere I have never been able to follow, and took my elk's voice with him."

He set his hand flat on the dull blade.

"I have spent twenty years thinking I lost my beast to a cold sign. The truth I can barely say aloud is that I lost it the moment I cared more about beating my friend than reaching him. The Silence was just the shape the cost took." He met Rin's eyes. "That is the mistake I trained you not to make. Whatever else you forget, do not forget that one."

c10_connect_the_dots.text:
The crowd above them surged — some other match, some other ending — and in the swell of it Rin's mind was already moving, the way it always did, fitting the new shapes against the old ones, because if you understood the shape of a thing you could survive it.

"The Masked Ace," Rin said slowly. "At the gate. The day we arrived. He was spinning that practice blade, and I felt — " they reached for it, the memory of that wrongness, the cold under-feeling that had crawled up their arms without a name. "I felt something off. Like a held breath that never let go. You went still. You wouldn't say why."

Tovan's mouth was a hard line.

"Because I knew the style the instant I saw it," he said. "There is exactly one school in the world that spins like that. It is not loud and it is not crude — it is precise and joyless and one degree off from the Silence at every turn, and it has exactly one author." He let the silence finish the sentence, then finished it anyway, because some things you must say out loud or they are not real. "Raze is Vehesal's. Taken as a child, raised on the cold creed, made into the heir of the man who silenced my elk. The Masked Ace is the Frost-Sage's blade pointed at the world."

Rin felt the whole story tilt and lock — the personal and the political snapping into one frame, Mira's half-formed suspicion about the rigged final and Tovan's twenty-year wound revealed as the same wound. "He's spinning his own beast into the cold," Rin said. "Mira saw it. He's going deaf to it. He doesn't even — does he know what he's losing?"

"No," Tovan said quietly. "That's the cruelest part. You can't grieve a thing you were raised to believe was never worth having."

c10_the_open_hand_teach.text:
Tovan rose then, the dull blade still in one hand, and crossed to the old worn dish at the center of the room. He set the silent elk-blade on its rim — not to launch it, Rin understood, but to have it near, the way you keep a quiet friend in the room while you say a hard thing.

"There's a sign I haven't taught you," he said. "Because I wasn't sure you were ready, and because teaching it means admitting why I know it." He lifted his empty hands and held them open, palms up, in a shape Rin had never seen him make — not the firm, asking curve of OPEN as Rin had drilled it a thousand times, but something looser, more frightening, a hand that was not reaching for anything at all. "The open-hand weave. Deep OPEN. The near-lost sign at the heart of true bonding."

Rin watched the empty hands and felt their stomach tighten the way it always did at OPEN, the one sign they could never make stick, the sign the no-name blade went flat and cold beneath every single time Rin reached for it and pulled back.

"Every other sign does something," Tovan said. "Listen gathers. Steady holds. Turn directs. Release calls. They're verbs — you act, the beast answers. But the open-hand isn't a verb. It commands nothing. It asks for nothing. It does only one thing." His voice was very gentle now. "It lets the beast in. All the way in. No grip, no guard, nothing held back, nowhere safe to retreat to if it hurts." He lowered his hands. "That's why it can't be faked, and why it can't be forced, and why the cold spinners can win a thousand matches and never once weave it. You cannot let someone in while keeping the exits counted."

c10_rin_thinks_useless.text:
Rin's first thought — and they hated themself a little for how fast it came — was that the open-hand weave was useless.

It was the kind of thought that had kept them alive. A sign that did nothing, that commanded nothing, that simply flung the door open and stood there unguarded while whatever was on the other side decided whether to come in or come for you — what good was that in a dish? In the duels ahead? Against a boy raised by the man who had weaponized exactly this, who would read an open door as an invitation to drive a cold sign straight through it?

They could imagine the open-hand the way you imagine a height you will not jump from. They could feel, in advance, the particular sick lurch of doing it — of reaching for the no-name blade not to win, not to direct, not even to ask, but only to be known by it, with nothing held back and no way to take it back if it turned out the blade did not want them after all. After fifteen years of practice at never doing precisely that.

"It won't help me beat him," Rin said. They meant it to sound certain. It came out closer to a plea.

Tovan didn't argue. He only looked at them, and there was no disappointment in it, which was somehow worse. "No," he agreed. "It won't help you beat anyone. That was never what it was for." He picked the dull blade up off the rim. "It's for the thing that's harder than winning. I'm not sure you'll need it. I hope you won't." A pause. "But I would rather you have it and not need it than need it on a dish someday and not have a name for the shape your hands should make."

c10_tone_choice.text: Rin stood at the rim of the worn old dish, the no-name blade a familiar weight in their hand and the open-hand weave a frightening new shape they did not yet know how to make. The Coach watched, patient, asking nothing. Outside, the crowd-tide rose and fell. They had one quiet hour and a sign that terrified them, and the question was only how to spend it.

choices.label: Try the sign now — reach for the blade, open, and see what answers.
Ask him to teach the shape first — understand it before you risk it.

c10_tone_try.text:
Rin set the chipped blade on the dish before they could talk themself out of it. They did not launch it — the open-hand was not for a spin, not yet — they only laid their hand near it, the way Tovan had laid his hand on the silent elk, and reached.

Not to ask. Not to direct. Just to open.

It was like stepping off a ledge in the dark. Every instinct Rin had spent a lifetime building threw itself against the motion — guard, hold, count the exits, keep something back. For one whole second they managed it anyway, hand open, heart open, nothing held, and the no-name core stirred under their palm, warmer than it had ever gone, a faint bright pressure like a held breath about to become a word —

— and then the old fear closed Rin's hand without asking permission, and the warmth guttered, and the blade went flat and quiet, and the almost-word was gone.

Rin pulled their hand back, breathing hard, as if they'd run a race. "I felt it," they said, shaken. "For a second. It was right there."

"I know," Tovan said softly. He had seen it too — Rin could tell from his face, the careful hope he was trying not to show. "That's further than I got the first hundred times. The hand closing — that's not failure. That's just the part of you that learned the world too young, doing its job." He almost smiled. "It'll learn a new one. It only needs a reason it believes."

c10_tone_ask.text:
"Show me the shape first," Rin said. "All of it. Before I — before I try it on the blade." Their voice was steadier than they felt. If they were going to leap off a ledge in the dark, they wanted to know exactly where their hands went on the way down.

So Tovan showed them. Not the launch, not the spin — just the hands, slow, over and over, the loose open palms that asked for nothing. He named the wrong versions as Rin made them: the OPEN that still gripped a little, the OPEN that kept a finger curled to take it all back. "There," he'd say. "You're still holding the door. Let it stand open even when it frightens you."

It frightened Rin a great deal. There was no blade involved, no beast, no risk at all beyond a man watching their empty hands — and still the old reflex fought every repetition, because the shape itself was the thing Rin had spent fifteen years not doing. By the twentieth try their hands had stopped fighting quite so hard. By the fortieth, the open palms felt less like falling and more like standing at an open window in winter: cold, exposed, but possible.

"Good," Tovan said at last, and the warmth in it caught Rin off guard. "You can't fake what you understand. And now you understand it. Whether you can do it when it costs you something — that's a different lesson, and the dish will have to teach it. But you'll know the shape your hands should make." He set the dull blade down. "That's not nothing. That's most of it."

c10_atonement.text:
They sat a while after that, the lesson settling, the crowd-roar thinning as the day's lower matches emptied the upper bowl. Rin turned the chipped no-name blade over in their hands and the Coach turned his silent one, and for a moment they were just two people in a worn old room with two blades that had each been left behind in their own way.

"Can I ask you something," Rin said, "and you tell me the true answer, not the kind one."

Tovan inclined his head.

"That morning. The dish-hall. You said you saw something in me." Rin kept their eyes on the chipped blade. It was easier than his face. "Was it really me? Or was it — " they made themself finish — "was I a way to fix what you did to your friend? Did you train me to atone?"

The honest thing about Tovan was that he did not rush to say no.

"At first," he said. "Some of it. Yes." Rin's chest tightened, and Tovan saw it and went on, gentle and unflinching at once. "I saw a kid talking to a chipped blade like it was the only friend they had, and I thought: there. There is the bond Vehesal swore was weakness, alive in the loneliest place in the city, and if I can wake it I can prove — to him, to the world, to myself — that I was right and the cost was worth it. So yes. At first you were partly that. An argument I needed to win."

c10_mentor_stirs.text:
"But that's not why I'm still here," Tovan went on, and now his voice had changed — roughened, careful, like a man stepping onto ice he is not sure will hold. "Somewhere along the road you stopped being an argument and started being a person I couldn't stand to see hurt. And then — " he stopped. Looked down at the silent elk in his hands. "Then you started making friends. That loud Kael boy. The Mira girl who reads everyone and can't read why she likes you. You let them in a half-step at a time, terrified the whole way, and I watched you do it."

He was quiet for a moment. When he spoke again it cost him visibly.

"Three weeks ago, in the stands, watching you laugh at something Kael said — I felt my elk stir."

Rin went still. "Stir."

"For the first time in twenty years. Not woken. Not a word. Just — a turning. Deep down, where I'd stopped letting myself listen. Like it heard something it recognized." His hands trembled, just slightly, around the dull blade, and he looked, suddenly, less like a sage and more like a man who had been afraid of one specific thing for two decades and had just admitted it out loud. "I haven't told anyone that. I haven't dared hope it meant anything. Hope is — " he gave a small, broken laugh. "Hope is the cold-style's whole argument against bonds, you know. That they only set you up to lose again."

Rin looked at the man who had been their fixed point, and saw, for the first time, how frightened he was.

c10_rin_comforts.text:
Rin had spent their entire life on the receiving end of this — the comforting, the steadying, the quiet hand on the shoulder from someone stronger. They did not know how to give it. They had never once practiced. Every exit in the room was still counted in the back of their mind, the door, the window, the long habit of being the one who needed nothing so no one could ever take anything away.

They did the open-hand anyway. Not with their hands — with the only other thing they had.

"It meant something," Rin said. Their voice shook and they let it. "It means something now. You didn't fail your friend, Coach. You loved him so much that twenty years later you're still trying to reach somebody — me, Raze, your own elk, all of it — instead of giving up and going cold like he did. That's not the man who silenced a beast." They swallowed. "That's the man still trying to wake one."

Tovan looked at them, and his weathered face did something Rin had never seen it do, and he did not bother to hide it.

"I'm not very good at this," Rin admitted. "Letting people — being let. Any of it. But you stayed." The word caught. "Everyone left. You stayed. And I don't know how to say thank you for that except badly, so. Thank you. Badly."

It was the most open thing Rin had ever said to a living person, and it had cost them every exit in the room, and the worst part — the part that would keep them up that night — was that it had not killed them. The floor was still there. The man was still there. The door, uncounted now, was just a door.

c10_win_it_all.text:
For a while neither of them spoke. The crowd was gone now, the upper bowl emptied, and the under-stair hall held only lamplight and dust and two blades and the enormous quiet of a thing finally said.

Then Tovan reached over and closed Rin's fingers around the chipped no-name blade, his big scarred hands over their small ones, the way you hand someone something you have decided to trust them with.

"Listen to me," he said. "There's a boy on the other side of this bracket who is exactly what you would have become if no one had ever stayed. He was taught that the open-hand is weakness, that the bond is a leash, that being alone is the same thing as being strong. The man who raised him is the man who silenced my elk, and they mean to prove, in front of the whole world, that everything you and I have built is a lie that just hasn't lost yet."

He tightened his grip, just once.

"You can't beat them with a colder blade. There isn't one. The only thing in this world the cold has never been able to answer is the thing you spent your life running from — and somewhere in these next days you're going to have to stop running and let it catch you, in front of everyone, with everything on the line." His eyes held Rin's, and under the grief in them, faint and stubborn and twenty years buried, was the thing he'd called too dangerous to feel. "I think you can. I think you're the one who can. So."

He let go of their hands.

"Win it all, Rin. Not the colder way. The harder one."

c11_summons.text:
Mira found them in the long shadow under the competitors' arch, where the day's heat had not yet reached. She did not announce herself. That was her way — she simply appeared at the edge of a thing, already three moves into a conversation no one else knew had started.

"You should see where the cold comes from," she said.

Rin had been watching Kael argue with a vendor over the price of skewered fish, losing badly and enjoying it. The morning had a borrowed ease to it, the kind Rin did not trust and could not stop wanting. Two rounds won. Two rivals who, against every law Rin had ever lived by, kept choosing to stand nearby. The wobble in their chest had gone quiet for almost a full day, and a quiet wobble always meant a wave was coming.

Here it was.

"The cold," Rin repeated.

"Raze. The Masked Ace." Mira's voice stayed level, but her fingers had gone still around Sumi's blade, and Rin had learned to read the fox's stillness the way they read a closing door. "I've watched his replays until my eyes ached. The micro-tells are everywhere. He isn't just winning. He's doing something to his beast." She paused. "And it traces back to one pavilion. Concord's. I think you should both see the man who taught it."

Kael drifted over, fish-grease shining on his grin, until he caught the look on Mira's face and the grin went out like a snuffed lamp. "Who died?"

"No one yet," Mira said. "That's rather the point."

Rin looked from one of them to the other — these two impossible people who had decided, without asking permission, to be theirs. The exit was right behind them, the way exits always were. Rin counted it, the old habit, and then did the new and terrifying thing instead. They stayed.
c11_summons.title: The Frost-Sage

c11_pavilion_door.text:
The Concord pavilion did not look like the rest of Coilspire.

The lower city was all warm clutter — chalk dust and hot metal, dishes worn smooth by ten thousand hands, vendors shouting over each other. The Tournament grounds had at least the honest sweat of competition. But the moment Rin stepped through the pavilion's tall doors, the temperature of the world changed. Not the air — that was held at some perfect, expensive cool — but something underneath it. The floor was pale stone polished to a mirror, and it threw their reflection back at them, small and out of place. Sleek banners hung in precise rows, each bearing the Concord spiral in cold silver: not the wild, hand-drawn spiral of the dish-halls but a thing measured by a compass, every loop identical, every loop perfect, and somehow the worse for it.

No one shouted here. Spinners practiced in glass-walled chambers along the hall, launching blades in eerie silence, their faces smooth and bored. There was no joy in the room. Rin realized that was what made the place feel wrong — not menace, exactly, but the total absence of delight. A whole hall of people doing the most wondrous thing in the world as if it were arithmetic.

"They make it look easy," Kael muttered, and there was something raw under the words. Rin glanced at him and understood: this was the world Kael's father wanted him in. This cold, gleaming approval he had chased his whole life. Kael stood a little straighter, the way a boy does when he is trying not to want something.

Mira led them deeper, past the glass, toward a single door at the hall's far end, set apart from the rest. She stopped before it. "He never spins anymore," she said quietly. "He fights through students now. Through Raze." She drew a breath. "His name is Vehesal."

c11_first_sight.text:
The room beyond was a study in white. White stone, white light, a long table bare of everything but a single dish — and that dish was empty, dustless, clearly unused, kept the way a man keeps a thing he has decided never to need again.

Vehesal stood at the window with his back to them, and even before he turned Rin felt it: the cold under-feeling, the same wrongness they'd sensed off Raze's practice blade weeks ago, only deeper, older, settled into the bones of the room. When he turned, Rin almost flinched, not from any cruelty in his face but from the lack of it. He was beautiful in the way winter is beautiful — frost-pale hair swept back from a high brow, eyes the grey of a sky that will not snow and will not clear, a stillness so complete it made the air around him feel loud.

"The orphan from the lower halls," he said. His voice was soft, courtly, almost kind. "And the wolf-boy from the failing club. And Mira." His gaze rested on her a moment longer. "My finest reader, wandering away from where her gifts are valued. I confess I'm disappointed, though not surprised. Talent is restless."

Mira said nothing. Rin saw the effort it cost her.

Vehesal came forward, unhurried, and stopped a courteous distance away — never crowding, always exact. "You've come to see the architect, I suppose. To find the monster behind the mask your friend wears." A faint smile. "I'm afraid you'll be disappointed there as well. There is no monster here. Only a man who learned, long ago, what the rest of you are still learning the hard way." He spread his thin hands, palms up, almost gentle. "That love is the weakest blade there is. Sit. Let an old man spare you some grief."

c11_doctrine_lead.text:
He did not raise his voice. That was the terror of him. Rin had braced for a villain who sneered, who threatened, who made the danger easy to hate — and instead got a man who spoke the way a kind teacher speaks to a slow student, patient and a little sad, certain he was doing them a mercy.

"Tell me," Vehesal said, settling into a chair as if they were all friends. "The chipped blade you carry. It answers you, doesn't it? Faintly. After all these years." He watched Rin's face and read whatever crossed it. "But it has never given you its name."

Rin's breath caught. They had told no one that. Not Kael, not Mira. Not even the Coach had been told in so many words.

"I know because I know what a held-back heart looks like," Vehesal went on, mild as snowfall. "You keep everyone a half-step away. You learned, as I learned, that the surest way to be left is to let someone close enough that leaving would hurt. So you made yourself useful and unattached, and you have survived. You are, in your way, a natural. The coldest spinner in this Tournament is the one who thinks they came here for warmth."

Kael shifted, his jaw tight. "Don't talk to them like that."

"I'm paying them a compliment." Vehesal did not look away from Rin. "A bond, child, is a leash. Need is the place where another hand reaches in and breaks you. I am offering you the only freedom there is — the freedom of needing no one." His grey eyes were almost tender. "I have spent my life teaching the young to put down a weight the world tells them is precious. Some of them weep with relief. Would you like me to show you why?"

c11_doctrine_choice.text: The room waited. Mira's stillness, Kael's coiled anger, Vehesal's patient cold — all of it bent toward Rin, toward how they would answer the most dangerous thing anyone had ever offered them: permission to stop trying.

choices.label: Answer quietly — name the wound in his own creed
Push back hard — refuse the mercy to his face

c11_ans_quiet.text:
Rin did not look away, but they did not rise to it either. They let the silence sit until it was theirs and not his.

"You keep a dish you never use," Rin said, nodding at the bare table. "Polished. Dustless. Like you can't quite throw it out."

Something moved behind Vehesal's eyes — quick, gone.

"A person who truly needed no one wouldn't keep it," Rin went on, the words coming slow, the way OPEN came slow, from somewhere under the armor instead of over it. "They wouldn't dust it. You're not free of the leash, sir. You're just standing very still so it won't pull." Rin's voice didn't shake. That surprised them most of all. "I know the difference. I've been doing it my whole life."

For a moment the courtly mask did not so much crack as flicker, the way a held breath flickers a flame. Vehesal's hand, resting on the table, drew very slightly back from the empty dish.

"You think you've seen something," he said, and the softness had thinned. "You've seen a habit. Not a wound."

"Maybe." Rin held his gaze. "But you flinched."

The word hung there. Outside the glass walls, a blade rang and died in someone's silent practice chamber, that particular thin sound a spin makes when it's failing — and for one strange instant Rin would have sworn the old man's eyes went to the noise before he mastered them. Mira's breath caught beside them. She had seen it too. The reader who read everyone, witnessing a tell she would not soon forget.

Vehesal folded his hands. When he spoke again the warmth was back, smooth and total, but Rin had felt the floor move under it.

c11_ans_hard.text:
Rin stood. Not in a temper — they had learned long ago that temper was just fear with the lid off — but because some answers should be given on your feet.

"No," they said. "I don't want your mercy."

Vehesal tilted his head, indulgent. "You don't yet understand the cost of —"

"I understand it better than you think." The words came hot and clear. "I grew up knowing exactly what you're selling. Want nothing, lose nothing. Need no one, get left by no one. I built my whole life on it before I could spell it." Rin's hands had curled at their sides. "And it works. That's the worst part. It works right up until you're standing alone in a white room you keep too clean, calling the loneliest thing in the world a freedom."

Kael made a low sound that might have been a laugh, fierce and proud, and stepped up beside them.

"You call a bond a leash," Rin said. "I called it that too. For fifteen years. Then two people I'd have crossed the street to avoid decided to stand next to me anyway, and I found out the leash was the only thing that ever held me up." They were breathing hard now. "You're not sparing anyone grief, sir. You're just teaching them to be as alone as you are, so it stops feeling like a thing that went wrong."

The room had gone very cold and very still. Vehesal's smile did not falter, but his eyes had hardened to grey ice, and somewhere far behind them — buried so deep Rin only caught it because they'd spent a lifetime watching for the flicker on other people's faces — something old and hurt looked out, just for a breath, and was put away.

"How loud you are," Vehesal said softly, "for someone the world has already left twice."

c11_raze_glimpse.text:
A door opened along the side wall, and Raze came in.

Rin had seen him before — masked, distant, spinning practice blades with that joyless, flawless perfection. Up close, in this white room, the wrongness of it had a different weight. He moved without a single wasted motion, the way Vehesal stood without one, and when he saw the three of them his masked face gave nothing at all. He carried his blade the way Rin had once carried the chipped one: as the only thing in the world that was his. The difference was that Rin had talked to theirs like a friend, and Raze, Rin understood with a cold drop in the stomach, had been taught never to talk to his at all.

"Raze," Vehesal said, and the boy stopped at once, perfectly. "Show them."

Raze launched. The blade dropped to the bare dish and spun, and the moment it did, Rin felt the cold sign close around it like a fist — not the open question of a true weave but a command, a clamp, a hand laid over a mouth. The blade obeyed beautifully. And under the obedience, faint and far and almost gone, Rin felt the beast inside it flinch.

It was the worst thing Rin had ever felt off a dish. Not pain, exactly. Distance. A creature being held one degree from a silence it could not climb back out of, going slowly, quietly deaf to the only person in the world who could reach it — and that person not even knowing its name anymore.

Rin's hand found their own chipped blade without deciding to. And for half a heartbeat, behind the eye-holes of the mask, Raze's gaze caught on that small, scarred, much-loved thing in Rin's grip — and held there, just a moment too long, like a starving person glimpsing a lit window.

c11_the_boy_under.text:
"Enough," Vehesal said, and Raze caught the blade out of its spin with a snap. The cold feeling vanished so abruptly that Rin swayed.

For an instant — only that — the Masked Ace stood with the dead-quiet blade cupped in both hands and his head bent over it, and the angle of his shoulders was not a champion's. It was the posture of a child who has been handed something he is not allowed to love. Then Vehesal said his name once more, lightly, and the boy straightened, and whatever had leaked through the mask was sealed again behind it.

Rin knew that sealing. They had done it ten thousand times themself, in the line at the orphan dish-hall, in the doorways of families who returned them. They knew it from the inside. That was the thing that turned their blood to water: not that Raze was a monster, but that Raze was them. The exact them they would have been if the Coach had never crouched down at dawn and seen something worth keeping. If no one had ever, even once, stayed.

"He has not lost a match in three years," Vehesal said, with the quiet pride of a man displaying a finely made clock. "He needs no one. He fears no loss, because there is nothing in that dish he is afraid to lose. That is what a champion is. That" — and here his grey eyes came back to Rin, almost gentle again — "is what defeats your warm little crowd of friends in the final, child, as surely as winter defeats a flower. Not because I wish you ill. Because I am right."

Kael's hands were fists. Mira's were very still. And Rin looked at the boy behind the mask and felt, instead of fear, something they had no name for yet — a pull, like kin recognizing kin across a great cold distance.

c11_the_rig.text:
Mira broke the silence, and her voice had the flat precision Rin had come to understand was how she held herself together. "You're so certain of the final," she said. "More certain than a man should be of a fight he hasn't seen."

Vehesal's smile did not change, and that, Rin thought, was its own answer.

"The Tournament has rules, child," he said. "Only true bonds may compete. The Bond-Wardens judge whether a beast answers freely." He let the words settle, each one polished smooth. "But Wardens are old, and few, and the council that seats them has grown… modern. Practical. Concord has friends among the judges now. Most of them." He spread his hands again, that gesture of reasonable regret. "When the final is judged, it will be judged by people who already understand which outcome is best for the sport. The kind of people who know a flower cannot be permitted to embarrass winter in front of the whole world. It would give the children ideas."

The air went out of Rin. "You're going to rig it."

"I am going to ensure the right lesson is taught," Vehesal corrected, untroubled. "There is one Warden who might object. The old woman, Oru. She still sees the old way, and she still has a tongue. But one voice on a council is not a vote. She has been outnumbered for years, and she has learned, as the wise do, to stay quiet." He looked almost sorry for her. "She will watch your bond lose and say nothing, because saying something has never once changed the count."

Mira had gone pale. This was the thing she'd traced through the ledgers and money and not wanted to be true. Hearing him say it aloud, calm as weather, was worse than any proof.

c11_the_message.text:
Vehesal rose, signaling the audience near its end, and crossed to where Rin stood. He did not loom. He never loomed. He simply came close enough to be heard quietly, and that nearness was its own kind of cold.

"You weave with an old man's hands," he said, studying Rin's grip on the chipped blade. "The way you hold the readying sign. The way you reach for OPEN and don't force it." His pale brows drew together, and for the first time something other than certainty crossed his face — recognition, and under it, a wound so old it had calcified into the bones of him. "There is only one man alive who still teaches that. I thought he was dead. I half hoped he was."

Rin said nothing. They had been told, from the beginning, that the Coach's past was the Coach's to tell.

"Tell Tovan," Vehesal said, and the name came out of him strangely, as if it cost something to shape, "that the Spirit-Sage's last student is climbing toward a dish they cannot win. Tell him I remember our final match very well. Tell him I have thought, every day for twenty years, about how easy it was." His grey eyes were terrible now, and terribly sad. "And tell him that this time he will watch the same lesson taught to a child he loves, and there will be nothing he can do but stand in the crowd and remember."

He stepped back. The courtly warmth flowed over the cold again like ice over a stream. "Thank you for visiting. Do give him my regards."

Rin's stomach had dropped through the polished floor. Tovan. The Coach had a name in this man's mouth, and the way he'd said it — old friend, old enemy, old grief — opened a door onto everything the Coach had only half told them.

c11_kael_refusal.text:
They were nearly to the tall doors when a Concord man in a silver-spiral coat stepped smoothly into Kael's path. Rin recognized the type: a recruiter, all teeth and warmth, the kind of man whose attention felt like sunlight until you noticed it only ever fell where it could grow something useful.

"Kael, isn't it? The wolf-blade." The man's smile was wide. "I've watched your Gauntlet runs. That aggression — beautiful instincts, just a little undisciplined. We could fix that. Cold style would make you unbeatable inside a year. Your father —" the man let the word land like a hook "— would finally see what you're worth."

Rin felt it the way you feel a blade leave the cord. This was the thing Kael had wanted his whole life. Approval with a Concord seal on it. The one currency his father might actually spend. Rin saw Kael's jaw work, saw the boy he'd been — performance-reviewed, never once told well done — lean toward the lit window of it.

Then Kael looked sideways. Not at the recruiter. At Rin.

"Last week," Kael said slowly, "I lost to this scavenger and their busted-up no-name blade. Worst day of my life, right up until it was the best one. You know what beat me?" His grin came back, but it had changed — it wasn't a costume anymore. "Not skill. They just... let me be a person instead of a wall to knock down. First time anyone ever did." He turned to the recruiter, and the swagger that had always been armor was suddenly something stronger, something real. "Your style goes deaf, friend. I felt it off the Ace from across the grounds. You're offering to make me unbeatable by killing the only thing that makes spinning worth a damn." He shrugged, easy as anything. "Hard pass."

The recruiter's smile froze. Kael was already walking, shoulder to shoulder with Rin, out into the warm and shouting day.

c11_chosen_side.text:
They didn't speak until the pavilion was well behind them and the ordinary noise of the grounds had folded back over their heads — vendors, launchers, the ringing clash of honest dishes, the warm chaos of a world that had not yet been made cold. Rin stood in it and breathed it in like someone surfacing.

"He knew about the blade," Rin said finally. "That it's never named itself. I never told anyone."

"He guessed." Mira's voice was quiet but certain again, the reader back in her element. "It's what he does — finds the held-back place in a person and presses it. He pressed mine too." She didn't say what he'd pressed. She didn't have to. The girl who feared she was nothing if she wasn't the smartest in the room had just walked out of a room with the smartest, coldest man alive, and stayed herself. "He's frightened, Rin. Underneath all of it. I read tells for a living and that man is the most frightened person I've ever stood across a table from. He's just had twenty years to build something to hide it in."

"His name is Tovan," Rin said. "The Coach. They know each other. They — " Rin stopped, the size of it landing. "That match he kept talking about. The lesson he taught. I think the Coach was there. I think the Coach was who he taught it to."

Kael let out a breath. "Then we ask him."

"He'll tell us when he tells us," Rin said, and was surprised to hear themself defending the Coach's silence — surprised, too, that the impulse was protective rather than guarded. "But the rig is real. The final's bought before we ever reach it." The wobble in their chest was back, fierce and cold. "They've already decided we lose."

c11_found_family.text:
Rin should have felt the old urge then — the urge that had run their whole life. Pull back. Hold the exit. Don't let these two close enough that the loss, when it came, would hurt. The Tournament was rigged; the cold creed was right; the smart kid's move was to make themself small and unattached and survive whatever came, alone, the way they always had.

They counted the feeling, the way they'd counted exits since before they could read. And then they let it go past them like a wave that finds you already standing.

Because here was the thing Vehesal, for all his terrible reading, had gotten wrong. He'd looked at Rin and seen a natural — a cold heart that only thought it wanted warmth. But Rin had just watched a wolf-boy turn down everything he'd ever chased, to stand in the noisy daylight beside a scavenger with a busted blade. They'd watched a girl who trusted nothing but patterns choose a person over the safe, smart, solitary thing. The leash Vehesal mocked was the only reason any of them was still standing in the sun instead of practicing in silence behind glass.

"He said we lose because love is weak," Rin said. They looked at Kael's fierce grin, at Mira's steady eyes, and the words came out level and sure. "Then we make him watch it not be."

"Now that," Kael said, throwing an arm across Rin's shoulders before Rin could flinch from it, "is the most reckless thing I've ever heard a scavenger say. I love it."

Mira almost smiled. Almost. "We'll need Oru," she said. "One old Warden and one old rule. It's thin."

"It's not nothing," Rin said. And for the first time, walking toward a final they had been told was already lost, Rin was not walking toward it alone — and that, more than any blade, was the thing that frightened and steadied them both at once.

c12_arrival.text:
The semifinal dish sat at the heart of the Coliseum like a held breath. Rin had spun on smaller stages, in the qualifier pits where the chalk was always damp and the rings rang flat, but this was the great floor itself, and standing at its edge felt like standing at the lip of a well that went down forever. Above them the tiers climbed into haze, thousands of faces stacked into a single roaring animal, and the air carried the smell Rin had known their whole life — hot metal, chalk dust, the sweet bite of friction-burn — only here it was vast, cathedral-vast, and it made the back of Rin's neck prickle.

The Frost-Sage's voice still lived somewhere behind their ribs. Bonds are leashes, Vehesal had said, in that pavilion of pale cold light, smiling the whole time. Need is weakness. I am only sparing the next generation the grief. Rin had walked out of there carrying the man's certainty like a splinter, because the worst part was how reasonable it had sounded — how much it had sounded like the rules Rin had lived by since they were small enough to be left.

They shook it off. Not now. Now there was a dish, and an opponent, and the old habit of counting the exits — there were six, Rin noted without meaning to, four at the floor and two up in the tiers. Kael was somewhere in the stands with Mira, the two of them bent over Mira's notes like conspirators. Pae would be up there too, leaning over the rail far enough to make the Coach nervous. Rin pressed the chipped blade flat against their palm. It was warm. It was always warm now, in a way it had not been a month ago, and Rin tried not to read too much into that, and failed.
c12_arrival.title: The Gentle Giant

c12_the_giant.text:
Then the far doors opened, and the crowd's roar changed pitch, and Rin understood what everyone had been warning them about.

Brakk did not walk into the arena so much as arrive at it, the way weather arrives. He was the largest spinner Rin had ever seen — not merely tall but built like a thing that had been quarried rather than born, shoulders that blocked the light of the floor-lamps, hands that could have palmed Rin's whole skull. He wore his launcher slung across his back like an afterthought, and when he lifted both arms to the roaring tiers the roar doubled, and he laughed, a sound Rin felt in the soles of their feet before they heard it.

"COILSPIRE!" he bellowed, turning a slow circle so every section got their moment. "You came to see a MOUNTAIN spin! Then watch this mountain MOVE!"

The crowd ate it up. Banners shook. Somewhere a drum started and a thousand voices found it.

Rin had braced for a brute. Everyone spoke of Brakk that way — the quarry-town giant, the powerhouse who flattened brackets by sheer force, the storm in a person-shaped vessel. And here he was, performing exactly that, every gesture sized for the back row. But Rin had spent fifteen years reading faces for the early warning of rejection, narrating other people's expressions before those expressions could be turned on them, and the habit did not switch off just because a man was three times their size. So while the giant played the giant, Rin watched the giant's eyes.

And the eyes were doing something the mouth wasn't.

c12_the_loneliness.text:
It was quick. A flicker, there and gone, in the half-second after the crowd's roar crested and before Brakk fed it again. In that gap his face did the thing Rin knew from the inside: it checked. It scanned the tiers, fast and hungry, looking for something specific in all that adoration and not finding it, and then it covered the not-finding with a bigger grin and a bigger gesture, because the grin was the only tool the world had ever handed him.

Rin had done that exact thing. Every dish-hall, every adopted-and-returned holiday, every time they made themself small and useful and funny so the room would keep them a little longer. You learn to be loud, or you learn to be quiet, depending on what the world decides you are. The world had decided Brakk was big, and so it had only ever offered him one role — the wall, the threat, the thing you cheer for from a safe distance and never sit beside. He had taken the role and made it enormous, and somewhere under all that thunder was a person nobody had ever bothered to meet.

Rin's chest did the wobble. Not fear, this time. Recognition.

The giant finished his circuit and planted himself at the dish's far rim, and up close he was even larger, a cliff-face of a person, and he looked down at Rin with frank curiosity. "You're the tailings kid," he said, and his speaking voice was almost gentle, a register lower and softer than the bellow, like a different man lived inside the loud one. "The chipped blade. They've all been talking about you."

"They talk about you more," Rin said.

Brakk's grin widened, but his eyes stayed careful. "They talk about my SIZE," he said. "That's not the same thing."

c12_stonewing.text:
He brought the blade out then, and the crowd hushed the way crowds do for a thing they revere.

It was beautiful. Where Rin's blade was chipped and no-name and the color of an old coin, Brakk's was broad and heavy and ringed with a wingspan motif worked into the metal — a storm-eagle, wings half-furled, that seemed to shift when the light moved across it. Stonewing. Even unspun, even resting in that enormous palm, the blade had a presence to it, a low steadiness, like a held note you could feel in your teeth.

"He's old," Brakk said, and he said he, not it, the way the Coach did, the way only true-bonded spinners did. "Older than me. We've been together since I was small enough to ride on a launcher." His thumb moved over the metal, an absent tenderness, the gesture of someone touching a thing they loved without thinking about it. "Oldest bond in the bracket, they say. Deepest, too." The grin flickered. "For all the good it does in a place that only counts who fell over last."

Rin felt the Coach's lessons settle over the moment. A vast gentle beast, the Coach had said once, describing a storm-eagle in the old texts, a creature built to ride the high currents for days, to climb on a thermal until the world below went soft and small — and Stonewing, bonded to a boy the world only ever met with fear, had learned to be exactly what his spinner had learned to be. Loud. Crushing. A roar where a soaring should be.

He only ever learned to roar, Rin thought, and the thought ached. He never learned to soar.

c12_what_he_wants.text:
"Can I tell you something?" Brakk said. He'd lowered his voice under the crowd's churn, so it was just the two of them at the rim, the giant bent slightly so Rin wouldn't have to crane. "Most spinners, when they face me, they do one of two things. They get scared and they spin careful, trying to outlast the big dumb mountain. Or they get angry and they spin reckless, trying to prove the mountain can fall." He shrugged, an avalanche of a movement. "Both of them, the whole match, they're spinning AT me. Like I'm a wall. Nobody spins WITH me."

He said it plainly, without self-pity, and that was somehow worse. Brakk was the most honest person in the bracket — a man with no gear for hiding what he felt, which made the little hiding he did manage all the sadder.

"What I want," Brakk went on, and his eyes found Rin's and held them, "is for somebody to give me everything they've got. Not because they're scared of losing. Because they think I'm worth their everything. One match where the person across the dish meets ME — not the size, not the noise, me — and gives me all of it, win or lose." He straightened, and the grin came back up like a shield going into place. "That's a stupid thing to want from a tournament, I know. You come here to win a crown."

"It's not stupid," Rin said, and meant it down to the floor.

Something crossed the giant's face — surprise, and under the surprise, a flinch of hope so quick he probably didn't know it showed. Rin knew that flinch. They had felt it in the dish-hall the morning a quiet stranger watched them talk to a blade like a friend and didn't laugh.

"The thing you're afraid of," Rin said, before they could stop themselves, "isn't losing. It's the day you can't win by being strong, and you find out whether anyone still wants you in the room."

Brakk went very still. The crowd roared on, oblivious. For a moment the largest spinner in the league looked at the smallest, and his mouth opened, and nothing came out.

c12_the_choice.text:
The referee's whistle cut the air — two minutes to the readying. Brakk shook himself, the way a man shakes off cold water, and resettled Stonewing in his grip. Whatever Rin had cracked open, he sealed it back up with a laugh, but the laugh was thinner now, and his eyes kept returning to Rin's face like he was checking whether the words had been real.

Rin had a choice to make, in the space of a breath, and it was the choice of how to give this giant the thing he had asked for — how to meet him.

choices.label: Stand tall, and tell him plainly that you respect his strength.
Match his power head-on, and promise him everything you've got.

c12_steady_branch.text:
Rin didn't raise their voice. They didn't have to. They stepped to the very rim of the dish, close enough that the giant had to look down at them, and they let the crowd's roar wash over both of them while they found the steady ground inside themselves — the place the Coach had taught them to stand on, low and rooted, the place where panic couldn't reach.

"I'm not going to spin scared of you," Rin said. "And I'm not going to spin angry at you. I came to a semifinal against the deepest bond in this bracket, and I'm going to treat it like what it is." They lifted the chipped blade so Brakk could see it — humble, nicked, no-name, the least impressive object on the entire floor. "Your strength is real. I respect it. I'm not going to pretend it isn't there so I can feel braver. I'm going to stand here and meet it on its feet, the whole way down."

Brakk stared at them. The honesty seemed to land somewhere he hadn't been touched in a long time, because his throat worked, and when he spoke his bellow had gone soft around the edges.

"You mean that," he said. It wasn't a question.

"I don't say things I don't mean," Rin said. "I never learned how."

The giant's whole face changed — the performed grin falling away, and under it, for one unguarded second, a person, plainly grateful and plainly afraid of being grateful. "All right," he said, low and rough. "All right, tailings kid. Then let's give these people something honest." He set his feet, mountain-solid, and Rin felt the steadiness of him answer the steadiness in their own chest — two people refusing, for once, to be the role the world assigned. The chipped blade was warm in Rin's hand, and steady, and ready.

c12_reckless_branch.text:
Something fierce and bright kindled in Rin's chest, and they let it. They grinned up at the giant — a real grin, not a careful one — and they spun the chipped blade once across their knuckles, fast, showing off, the way they never let themselves show off.

"You want everything I've got?" Rin said. "Then you'd better hold onto that mountain. Because I'm not going to outlast you, and I'm not going to chip away at you. I'm going to come straight at you with all of it — every bit of spin in this beat-up little blade — and we are going to find out exactly how big you are."

For a heartbeat Brakk looked startled. Then the startle broke open into pure delight, a grin so wide and so genuine it transformed his whole quarried face, and he threw back his head and laughed — not the performance-laugh he fed the crowd, but a deep helpless gust of joy, the laugh of a man who has waited years for one specific sentence and finally heard it.

"HA!" The bellow rolled across the floor and the tiers caught it and roared it back. "Did you HEAR that?" he shouted to no one, to everyone, slapping his enormous chest. "The little one's going to come straight at me! Spirits, FINALLY!" He leveled his gaze back down at Rin, and his eyes were shining, actually shining. "Don't you dare hold back. You hold back on me and I'll never forgive you."

"I won't," Rin promised, and the promise had teeth. The fierce thing in their chest had spread down their arms, into the warm metal of the blade, and the blade answered it — a quickening, a brightness, the no-name core leaning toward the fight not to win but to be fully, recklessly given. Whatever happened next, Rin would meet this giant with all of it, and let the chips fall. Let them fall like thunder.

c12_readying.text:
The referee strode to the dish's center, arm raised, and the great roaring animal of the crowd went, by degrees, quiet — that particular held-breath hush that only a packed stadium can make, forty thousand people deciding at once to stop breathing so they don't miss the start.

Rin and Brakk took their marks at opposite rims. Across the floor the giant rolled his shoulders, settled Stonewing into his launcher, and bowed his head over the blade for a moment — and Rin recognized the gesture, because it was the same one the Coach had taught them. He was readying. He was beginning the signs.

Rin lifted their own launcher, fit the chipped blade to the cord, and began to weave. Listen, first — quieting the noise, the crowd, the splinter of the Frost-Sage's voice, until there was only the faint warm presence in the metal, the friend that had never left. Steady — finding the low rooted place, the floor under the floor. Then they reached for the readying sign and felt the core rise to meet their hand, eager, already humming.

Across the dish, Stonewing began to glow.

It was faint at first, a charge gathering along the eagle-wing motif, and then it built — Rin could feel it across the open floor, a pressure in the air like the moment before a storm breaks, the static lift that raises the hairs on your arm. The oldest, deepest bond in the bracket was waking up, and it was vast, and Rin understood with a thrill of fear and wonder that they had never spun against anything remotely this strong.

The referee's arm came down.

"Spinners! Ready your blades!"

Rin set their stance. Brakk, across the dish, met their eyes and grinned — and this time Rin grinned back.

c12_launch.text:
"THREE!"

The count cracked across the silent arena and the silence somehow deepened, every soul in the tiers leaning in.

"TWO!"

Rin felt the cord taut under their fingers, the chipped blade trembling against it like a living thing straining toward the dish. Warm. So warm now. They thought, the way they always thought in this last suspended second, of the dawn dish-hall where they'd first spun this blade alone, the one place the wobble in their chest went quiet — and they thought, for the first time, that the quiet didn't only come from being alone anymore. It came from this, too. From a giant across a dish who wanted to be met. From three friends somewhere up in the roaring dark who had chosen, freely, to stand and watch.

"ONE!"

Brakk's launcher creaked as the great blade wound to its peak. The static lifted the chalk dust off the dish in a slow shining veil. Rin drew one breath, all the way down to the steady place, and let everything they were gather in the single point where the cord met the core.

They met the giant's eyes one last time across the trembling floor. And together — the mountain and the tailings kid, the deepest bond and the no-name one, two people who had both spent their whole lives believing strength was the only thing that ever made them worth keeping — together they cried the words every spinner in the world is taught before they are taught to walk:

"SPIRITS, FLY!"

The blades left the cords. Stonewing came down into the dish like a thunderhead falling, and the whole Coliseum shook, and Rin's chipped blade dove to meet it — and the semifinal began.

c13_into_the_dish.text:
The launch had already happened. That was the strange thing about the moment after the count, the way the world snapped from held breath to motion with no seam between them — one instant the dish was a flat silver eye and the next it was a storm.

Rin felt the chipped blade leave the launcher the way they always felt it: not in the hands but in the chest, a small tug behind the ribs, as if some part of them had been thrown out across the dish along with the no-name beast. It bit into the metal and held, spinning low and lean, the frayed cord Pae had tied around the launcher still warm where Rin's thumb had pressed it for luck.

Across from them, Brakk's storm-eagle hit the dish like weather.

There was no other way to describe it. Stonewing came down in a wide arc and the whole basin rang — a deep bronze note that Rin felt in their teeth, in the soles of their feet, in the loose change of breath the crowd let go all at once. The giant had not even bothered to crouch into a ready stance. He stood at his end with his arms loose and his chin up and a grin splitting his broad face, watching his blade roar across the steel like a boy watching his own kite catch a gale.

'There you are,' Brakk boomed, delighted, as though they had been hiding. 'Come on, little spinner. Don't make me wait.'

Rin set their feet. The wobble in their chest had not gone quiet — but for once, oddly, it did not feel like fear. It felt like the held note before thunder.
c13_into_the_dish.title: Thunder and Heart

c13_the_giant_at_play.text:
Rin had spent the whole tournament reading faces for the moment they would turn. It was a habit older than memory: watch the eyes, watch the mouth, catch the small contraction that came a half-second before a person decided you were not worth keeping. Rin could narrate a room of strangers like weather, and they were almost never wrong.

Brakk broke the habit entirely.

There was nothing under his grin. That was what undid Rin's vigilance — not warmth disguising a wound, the way Kael's swagger had hidden a boy who'd never been told 'well done,' not Mira's stillness filtering out everything that might cost her. Brakk simply meant it. He was having the best afternoon of his life. Every time Stonewing's spin lifted a curl of chalk-bright wind off the dish, the giant laughed from somewhere deep in his chest, and the laugh was so plainly, helplessly glad that Rin felt their own guard slipping like a foot on wet stone.

'You're quick,' Brakk called, watching the chipped blade thread the eagle's wake. 'Quicker than the recordings. I knew it.' He thumped a fist against his own chest. 'I told Stonewing — I said, this one fights with the whole of them. Not just the hands.'

The storm-eagle keened, and the sound rolled up the tiers and came back as the crowd's answering noise.

This was the oldest bond in the bracket. Rin had been told so, but knowing a thing and standing inside it were different. Brakk and Stonewing did not look like a spinner and a beast. They looked like one large warm creature that happened to be standing in two places, and the joy ran between them in both directions, freely, the way Rin had never once let anything run.

c13_the_eagle_that_only_roars.text:
Stonewing wheeled and came again, and the second pass was worse than the first.

Not crueler — Brakk did not have a cruel pass in him — but heavier, a downhill avalanche of a blade that drove Rin's smaller core toward the rim. Rin gave ground, riding the wash of it, and felt their own beast shudder against the impact and steady. The no-name core was holding. For now.

What caught Rin, in the half-second before the clash, was the shape inside the blur. Every beast left a ghost in the spin if you knew how to look, and Stonewing's was enormous — a thunderhead with wings, a thing built to ride the high cold air above the mountains where Brakk came from. It should have been soaring. It should have hung over this dish like a god and stooped from the clouds.

Instead it roared and roared and stayed low, hammering side to side along the steel, all that vast strength pressed flat into the only thing it had ever been allowed to do. The Coach's words from a training hall a lifetime ago surfaced unbidden: a beast is a two-way mirror of its spinner. Stonewing only ever learned to roar because the world only ever asked Brakk to be loud. A quarry-town boy too big to be anything but feared, who learned to thunder because no one offered him a quieter way to be wanted.

Rin's chest did the thing it had been doing all tournament — the recognition that landed like a blow. They knew this. They knew, exactly, what it was to make yourself into the one shape the world would accept and call it your whole self.

The blades closed. The dish trembled.

choices.label: Unleash your spirit-beast and meet the storm head-on
Read his charge, then turn it against him
Defend, ride the rim, and outlast the thunder

c13_unleash_b.text:
Rin stopped giving ground.

It went against every instinct they had — against a lifetime of slipping sideways out of the path of anything large enough to hurt — but Brakk did not deserve to be slipped away from. He deserved to be met. So Rin set their feet at the very lip of the rim, drew the breath all the way down, and wove RELEASE.

The no-name beast came up out of the chipped blade like a held cry finally let go. It had no name to call, but it had Rin's whole heart behind it, and that turned out to be enough to make the small core blaze. The blade surged off the rim and drove straight into the heart of Stonewing's storm — not around it, not under it, but into it, the way you walk into a wave instead of letting it knock you down.

The two beasts met in the center of the dish and the sound was enormous. Rin felt the impact travel up through their feet and rattle their teeth and ring in the old chip on the blade's edge. For one impossible second the chipped orphan core held the line against the largest spirit in the bracket, the two of them grinding wing to wing, and the crowd came up off the benches in a single roar.

Brakk's face split with pure astonished delight. 'YES!' he bellowed, and there was no fear in it, none at all, only a joy so total it was almost holy. 'Yes — like THAT — don't you dare hold back from me!'

Rin did not hold back. For the first time in their life, against the one opponent who would never punish them for it, they gave everything and kept nothing in reserve.

c13_unleash_b2.text:
The exchange could not last and both of them knew it. Stonewing was the deeper well; in a straight contest of power the storm-eagle would always have one more gale in it than a scavenged blade could answer.

But Rin had not unleashed to win a contest of power. They had unleashed to be honest. And the no-name beast, blazing brighter than it ever had in any qualifier, found the seam Brakk's joy had left open — the single instant where the giant, lost in the sheer delight of being met, leaned his whole storm forward to meet Rin's whole heart.

Rin pivoted at the rim and let Stonewing's own momentum carry it past.

The storm-eagle overran the center, talons of pressure raking empty steel, and Brakk laughed even as it happened, even as he saw it happen, because it was beautiful and it was fair and it was exactly the thing he had come all this way to feel. Rin's chipped blade caught the wash of the overrun and rode it like a leaf on the front of a flood, around and behind, into the open space the storm had left.

Stonewing's spin guttered. The deep bronze note that had filled the basin dropped a half-step, then another, the unmistakable dying ring of a core running out of dish to run in.

The giant's blade slowed, wobbled once with a sound like a sigh, and lay down.

For a moment nobody in the entire coliseum made a sound. Then Brakk threw back his head and laughed at the painted ceiling, arms wide, as though he had just been handed the finest gift of his life — which, in a way Rin did not yet understand, he had.

c13_counter_b.text:
Rin let the storm come.

It was the hardest discipline they had — to stand at the rim with an avalanche bearing down and do nothing, to trust that the right answer was not motion but timing. Mira would have approved. Read the pattern, she would have said, in that clean economical way of hers. Strength this large is also strength this committed. A thing that big cannot change its mind quickly.

So Rin watched. Not the blade — the spinner. Brakk's eyes, Brakk's shoulders, the way his weight rocked forward a fraction before each of Stonewing's downhill passes, telegraphing the line of the charge a half-beat before it came. The giant hid nothing. He had never in his life had a reason to. Every glorious, thunderous attack arrived stamped with its own address.

Stonewing reared for the big pass, the one meant to drive Rin off the steel for good — and Rin, who had read it in Brakk's shoulders a full breath before it launched, was already moving to the one place the storm could not turn in time to reach.

The chipped blade slid inside the arc of the charge. Close — close enough that Rin felt the wind of the eagle's wings comb past their core like a hand — and tucked into the dead air at the storm's own center, the still eye that every storm carries and cannot strike.

Brakk's grin did not falter. If anything it widened, a slow dawning wonder spreading across his huge face. 'Oh,' he breathed, and the word was almost tender. 'Oh, you READ me.'

c13_counter_b2.text:
From the eye of the storm, Rin worked.

This was the part Mira could have calculated and could never have done — because the counter only finished if Rin was willing to stay that close, inside the giant's reach, trusting a person large enough to crush them not to. Every survival instinct Rin owned screamed to break away to safe distance. Rin ignored all of them and stayed.

Stonewing wheeled, hunting the small blade that had vanished into its own blind spot, and each turn of the great beast cost it spin — a storm spends itself fastest when it has nothing to strike. Rin nudged the chipped core a hand's width whenever the eagle came near, never enough to clash, only enough to make Stonewing turn again, and again, and again, until the deep bronze roar began to thin at the edges.

Brakk understood what was happening. Rin watched the understanding cross his face — not anger, never anger, but a kind of marveling respect that made his eyes go bright and wet at the corners. He could have raged against it. Instead he laughed, low and astonished, and said, 'You're not stronger than me, little spinner. You're not. You just — you wanted it more carefully.'

Stonewing's spin failed in the center of the dish, the great wings folding down into the blur, the bronze note sighing out into silence. The storm-eagle's blade rocked twice and went still.

Rin's chipped core wobbled in the sudden quiet, scarred and spinning and alive, the last blade turning in the whole vast hush of the coliseum. Brakk stared at it like a man looking at something he had waited his entire life to see and had stopped believing existed.

c13_defend_b.text:
Rin chose to outlast the thunder.

There was no shame in it and Brakk, of all opponents, would never have called it cowardice — but it took a different kind of nerve than meeting power with power. It meant accepting, pass after pass, that you would not strike back; that you would simply refuse to be moved for longer than the storm could keep raging. It meant making yourself into the one thing the lower-city dish-halls had built Rin to be: hard to get rid of.

So Rin rode the rim and held.

Stonewing came and came. Each pass drove the chipped blade toward the edge and each time Rin bled off the force at an angle, sliding along the lip of the dish instead of being thrown over it, the cracked little core groaning with the strain and not, quite, failing. The crowd did not understand at first. They wanted clashes, collisions, the bronze roar of impact — and Rin gave them none of it, only a small scarred blade that would not, would not, would not go down.

Brakk understood before the crowd did. Rin saw it land on his face around the fifth pass: the slow realization that the little spinner was not running and was not breaking, that they had decided to weather him, and that the weathering was a kind of respect deeper than any clash. His grin changed. It went, for a moment, almost soft.

'You'd just stand there,' he said, wondering, 'and take everything I have. The whole storm. And still be standing.' He shook his great head. 'Spirits. Most people run from the storm. You're going to make me run out of it.'

c13_defend_b2.text:
A storm is only as deep as the air that feeds it. Brakk's was the deepest in the bracket — but it was not bottomless, and a beast that throws its whole strength at a thing it cannot move begins, eventually, to spend itself on nothing.

Rin counted the passes the way they had once counted exits, a quiet metronome under the roar. Each one came a fraction slower than the last. Each landed a fraction lighter. Stonewing was magnificent and Stonewing was tiring, and the chipped blade — too stubborn to die, scavenged out of a bin because nobody else had wanted it, the one thing in Rin's life that had never been taken back — simply kept turning.

The no-name beast held the rim and did not flinch.

On the ninth pass the storm-eagle came down and the bronze note that had filled the basin all match finally cracked. Stonewing's spin staggered, caught, staggered again. Brakk's whole frame leaned with it, willing his oldest friend through one more turn, and the love in that lean was so naked that Rin's throat tightened in the middle of the dish.

The storm-eagle laid itself down gently, the way a tired thing lies down. No crash. Just a slowing, and a settling, and the great wings folding into stillness.

Rin's blade spun on alone at the rim — wobbling, scarred, last. The whole coliseum exhaled at once, a sound like a tide going out, and then began, somewhere in the high tiers, to roar.

Brakk looked at the small unbroken blade for a long moment. When he lifted his eyes to Rin, they were shining.

c13_the_turn.text:
The marshal raised the flag. The match was called. And Brakk — the largest spinner Rin had ever seen, the powerhouse of the league, the man whole crowds were afraid of — stood very still at his end of the dish with his hands open at his sides and his great shoulders sloping, and for one terrible second Rin understood that he was bracing himself.

This was the part Rin had not expected to recognize. The whole tournament, every opponent at the moment of their loss had shown Rin the same flinch underneath — Kael bracing to be mocked, Mira bracing to be diminished — and here it was again on the kindest face in the bracket. Brakk had lost. And somewhere under the joy, in the place he never let anyone see, the giant was waiting to find out whether losing meant he was done being wanted.

That secret fear: that the day he could not win by sheer power was the day no one would have a use for him.

Rin knew that fear in their own bones. They had carried its cousin their whole life — make yourself useful, make yourself strong, make yourself necessary, because if you are not necessary they will send you back. Rin had read it in Brakk's blade, in the eagle that only roared, and now they read it in the careful stillness of a man waiting to be left.

Rin did not go to the marshal. They did not raise their hands to the crowd. They crossed the dish — the whole wide silver length of it, every exit forgotten — and stopped in front of the giant, and looked up, and up, into a face that was trying so hard to keep smiling.

c13_the_thing_he_never_heard.text:
'That,' Rin said, 'was the best match of my life.'

Brakk's smile wavered, uncertain, waiting for the part that always came after — the polite turning-away, the handshake that was really a goodbye.

Rin did not give it to him. Instead they said the thing. The thing they had never once been able to say to themself, the thing the whole tournament had been quietly teaching them, the thing no one had ever bothered to tell the gentle giant in the whole loud lonely length of his life.

'You'd still be the best part of this,' Rin said, 'even if you'd won. Even if you'd put me through the rim in the first pass and I'd never landed a hit. I wouldn't want you in my corner because you're strong, Brakk.' The words came up from somewhere Rin kept locked, and saying them out loud was like prying open a door rusted shut for years — it hurt, and the air on the other side was clean. 'I'd want you there because it's you. Win or lose. That's the whole reason.'

For a moment the giant simply stared, as if Rin had spoken in a language he had heard about but never believed was real.

Then Brakk's face came apart.

Not in grief — in something far larger, the way a dam does not so much break as finally, gratefully, let go. His eyes spilled over and he made no move to hide it, this enormous man weeping openly in the center of the dish in front of forty thousand people, and laughing at the same time, a great wet helpless laugh that shook his whole frame.

c13_undone.text:
'What a champion,' Brakk got out, between the laughing and the weeping, his voice cracking clean down the middle. 'What a — spirits, what a WORTHY champion.'

And then he caught Rin up.
